dense_only.question: Why can building a heap from an array be faster than inserting each element one at a time?
dense_only.ground_truth: Bottom-up heap construction performs most work near the top but many nodes are near the bottom and require little sinking, giving linear total time rather than repeated logarithmic inserts.
dense_only.answer:
Building a heap from an array can be faster than inserting each element one at a time because the BuildHeap operation runs in linear time, O(n), whereas each insertion incurs an O(log n) cost.

Specifically, when inserting elements one at a time into a heap, each new element must be added at the end and then "bubbled up" to maintain the heap property, which takes O(log n) time per insertion [Source 1, 4, 6]. In contrast, the BuildHeap operation constructs the heap in-place from the entire array and takes advantage of the fact that many nodes are already near their correct position, so the "bubble down" operations performed during BuildHeap collectively take only O(n) time, which is asymptotically faster than performing n insertions each costing O(log n) [Source 5].

Thus, although each insertion has a logarithmic cost, building the heap all at once is overall more efficient because it avoids this repeated bubbling up and makes use of the heap structure more globally to organize elements faster.

In short:  
- Inserting n elements one-by-one: O(n log n) total  
- Building the heap from an array all at once: O(n) total  

Therefore, BuildHeap is faster due to its linear time complexity compared to repeated insertion [Source 5].

The idea of a dynamic array is to keep the fundamental array property of storing items in a contiguous memory block, but allow the array to expand when the existing array is full. One might think that this expansion is easy, as we can always increase the size of an array by giving it ownership of some memory blocks after its current endpoint. But of course that memory might be already allocated for a different use, and if it is then the existing array cannot simply be expanded.

Instead, we will do the only thing we can, and allocate a separate and bigger block of memory for the array, copying over all existing elements, and then inserting the new element. Worst-case running time of dynamic arrays

For the purposes of analysing the running time of this data structure, we will only count the number of array accesses made. This actually allows us to compute an exact number for the cost, which will be useful in the following sections.

For now, suppose we have a dynamic array where all n allocated spots are full. We note that the final two steps involve just one array access (inserting the new item x ), while the code executed in the if block has exactly 2 n accesses: accessing each of the n items in the old array and copying each item to the new array.

So we have a worst-case running time of 2 n + 1 = O ( n ) array accesses. This upper bound does not seem very impressive: AVL trees were able to support insertion in worst-case Q ( log n ) time, for instance. So why should we bother with dynamic arrays at all? The intuition is that this linear worst-case insertion is not a truly representative measure of the efficiency of this algorithm, since it only occurs when the array is full. Furthermore, if we assume the array length starts at 1 and doubles each time the array expands, then the array lengths are always powers of 2 . This means that This 'different use' might even be external to our program altogether!

While this does cause us to ignore the cost of the other operations, all of them are constant time, and so focusing on the number of array accesses won't affect our asymptotic analysis.

Let us summarize TLB activity during our ten accesses to the array: miss , hit, hit, miss , hit, hit, hit, miss , hit, hit. Thus, our TLB hit rate , which is the number of hits divided by the total number of accesses, is 70%. Although this is not too high (indeed, we desire hit rates that approach 100%), it is non-zero, which may be a surprise. Even though this is the first time the program accesses the array, TLB performance gains benefit from spatial locality . The elements of the array are packed tightly into pages (i.e., they are close to one another in space ), and thus only the first access to an element on a page yields a TLB miss.

Also note the role that page size plays in this example. If the page size had simply been twice as big (32 bytes, not 16), the array access would suffer even fewer misses. As typical page sizes are more like 4KB, these types of dense, array-based accesses achieve excellent TLB performance, encountering only a single miss per page of accesses.

Dynamic arrays

The idea of a dynamic array is to keep the fundamental array property of storing items in a contiguous memory block, but allow the array to expand when the existing array is full. One might think that this expansion is easy, as we can always increase the size of an array by giving it ownership of some memory blocks after its current endpoint. But of course that memory might be already allocated for a different use, and if it is then the existing array cannot simply be expanded.

Instead, we will do the only thing we can, and allocate a separate and bigger block of memory for the array, copying over all existing elements, and then inserting the new element. We show below one basic implementation of this approach, where A has three attributes: array , a reference to the actual array itself; allocated , the total number of spots allocated for array ; and size , the number of filled spots in array . For this implementation, we choose an 'expansion factor' of two, meaning that each time the array is expanded, the memory block allocated doubles in size.

dense_only.question: Why does the AVL height-balance property help guarantee logarithmic search time?
dense_only.ground_truth: The balance condition prevents the tree from becoming too skewed, so the height grows logarithmically with the number of nodes and search follows a logarithmic-length path.
dense_only.answer:
The AVL height-balance property requires that for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. This constraint ensures that the tree remains balanced, preventing it from becoming excessively skewed, which could degrade search efficiency.

Because each node is balanced in this way, the overall AVL tree stays close to a complete binary tree in shape, which has minimal height for a given number of nodes. Formally, it has been proven (Lemma 3.5) that an AVL tree with \( n \) nodes has height at most approximately \( 1.441 \log n \). Since the search time in a binary search tree is proportional to its height, this balance property ensures searches run in logarithmic time in the worst case.

Thus, by maintaining the AVL invariant during insertions and deletions through local restructuring (rotations), AVL trees guarantee that the height—and therefore the search time—remains logarithmic in the number of nodes [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4].

4 Dictionaries, Round Two: Hash Tables

We now look at a completely different approach for implementing dictionaries. To get warmed up, consider the following scenario: all of the key-value pairs we wish to store have keys that are numbers 0 through K -1. In this case, we can store these pairs inside an array of length K , and achieve constant time search, insertion, and deletion simply by storing each value at the array index corresponding to its key!

This technique is known as direct addressing , and works well when the number of possible keys (and hence total number of pairs) is small. However, array addressing is only constant time if the entire array has been allocated in memory. Thus as K grows larger, even if the running time of the dictionary operations stays constant, the space required grows linearly in K . In this chapter, we will study a generalized version of direct addressing known as hashing , which allows us to store key-value pairs when the keys aren't necessarily numbers, and using much less space than the number of all possible keys.

dense_only.question: What is the purpose of rotations in AVL trees?
dense_only.ground_truth: Rotations restore height balance after updates while preserving the binary search tree ordering of keys.

The purpose of rotations in AVL trees is to restore the balance property (the AVL invariant) after insertions or deletions that cause the balance factor of a node to become less than -1 or greater than 1. Since insertions or deletions can only change the height of a subtree by at most 1, an imbalance at a node must have a balance factor of either 2 or -2. Rotations are constant-time restructuring procedures that rearrange parts of the tree locally to restore the balance without violating the binary search tree property.

Specifically:
- A **right rotation** is used when the left subtree is too tall compared to the right subtree, and it helps to reduce the height difference by rotating nodes so that the subtree is more balanced.
- A **left rotation** is symmetric and used when the right subtree is too tall.
- In more complex cases where subtree heights follow particular patterns (e.g., when a subtree "B" is "too tall" in the left-right or right-left imbalance cases), double rotations like left-right or right-left rotations are applied to restore balance.

Overall, rotations maintain the AVL invariant, which requires that the balance factor at every node lies between -1 and 1, ensuring the tree remains balanced for efficient search, insertion, and deletion operations [Sources 4, 5, 6, 8].

Thus, rotations are essential to keeping AVL trees balanced after updates, ensuring the height remains logarithmic in the number of nodes.

dense_only.question: Compare a naive binary search tree and an AVL tree.
dense_only.ground_truth: A naive BST can become highly unbalanced and have linear-height operations. An AVL tree maintains balance through rotations, keeping operations logarithmic.
dense_only.expected_source_hint: Chapter 3, Naive BSTs and AVL Trees
dense_only.answer:
A naive binary search tree (BST) inserts new keys as leaves without restructuring the tree, so its shape depends heavily on the order of insertions. This can lead to very imbalanced trees with height up to the number of nodes, which degrades search, insertion, and deletion performance [Source 4].

An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that maintains an AVL invariant: for every node, the balance factor (defined as the height of the right subtree minus the height of the left subtree) is between -1 and 1. This AVL balancing condition ensures that the tree remains balanced after insertions and deletions by performing rotations to fix imbalances [Source 1].

Because of the balance condition, the height of an AVL tree with n nodes is tightly bounded, at most about 1.441 log n for large n, guaranteeing logarithmic height [Sources 3, 8]. Consequently, all AVL operations (search, insertion, deletion) run in worst-case logarithmic time, which is an improvement over naive BSTs that can degrade to linear time in the worst case [Source 6].

In summary:
- Naive BST: simple insertion, no balancing, height can be linear in n, worst-case operations O(n).
- AVL tree: maintains strict balancing via rotations, height O(log n), worst-case operations O(log n).

Thus, AVL trees avoid the poor worst-case performance of naive BSTs by enforcing and maintaining the balance invariant during updates.

4 Dictionaries, Round Two: Hash Tables

We now look at a completely different approach for implementing dictionaries. To get warmed up, consider the following scenario: all of the key-value pairs we wish to store have keys that are numbers 0 through K -1. In this case, we can store these pairs inside an array of length K , and achieve constant time search, insertion, and deletion simply by storing each value at the array index corresponding to its key!

This technique is known as direct addressing , and works well when the number of possible keys (and hence total number of pairs) is small. We now look at a completely different approach for implementing dictionaries. To get warmed up, consider the following scenario: all of the key-value pairs we wish to store have keys that are numbers 0 through K -1. In this case, we can store these pairs inside an array of length K , and achieve constant time search, insertion, and deletion simply by storing each value at the array index corresponding to its key!

Thus as K grows larger, even if the running time of the dictionary operations stays constant, the space required grows linearly in K . dense_only.question: How does closed addressing handle collisions in a hash table?
dense_only.ground_truth: Closed addressing stores colliding keys in a secondary structure, commonly a linked list or bucket, at the same table index.
dense_only.answer:
Closed addressing handles collisions in a hash table by storing, at each array element, a pointer to a linked list of key-value pairs rather than a single value. When multiple keys hash to the same index (a collision), all such keys and their values are inserted into the linked list associated with that index. This way, collisions are "sidestepped" by chaining all colliding elements together in the linked list. 

When searching or deleting, the algorithm traverses the linked list at the hash index to find the correct key-value pair. This approach is also known as "chaining" [Source 1].

In this chapter, we will study another form of algorithm analysis that offers a new type of refinement of worst-case analysis. To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

One can get around this problem by storing the hash table with a data structure that uses dynamically-allocated memory like a linked list or AVL tree, but then we lose the constant-time addressing feature that we get from storing items in a contiguous block of memory. In this chapter, we will study a variant of arrays called dynamic arrays , which we use to implement a resizable collection of items that supports constant-time addressing and 'efficient' insertion of new items. We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

To cause this worst-case behaviour in practice, a malicious user would study the hash function used and determine such a set of colliding keys. You might be tempted, then, to keep your hash function a secret so that no one can figure out these collisions. But a reliance on such an approach only goes so far as how able you (and your colleagues) are in keeping this secret.

But let us take from this the insight that a malicious user needs to know which hash function is being used in order to purposefully generate large numbers of collisions. Rather than keep the hash function a secret, we simply use a set of hash functions, and allow our algorithm to pick randomly which one to actually use, without making its choice public. To 'normal' users, the hash table behaves exactly as expected, regardless of which hash function is used. In other words, the interface of the hash table has not changed. But even if a malicious user knows the whole set of hash functions, she does not know which one is actually being used by the hash table, and in principle cannot determine how to generate collisions.

Of course, if we picked a poor set of hash functions, it might be possible that each one has a huge number of collisions, or that the same keys collide for all or most of the functions. So we certainly need some restriction on the hash functions that can go into this set; we make this idea precise in the following definition.

We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

To cause this worst-case behaviour in practice, a malicious user would study the hash function used and determine such a set of colliding keys. You might be tempted, then, to keep your hash function a secret so that no one can figure out these collisions. But a reliance on such an approach only goes so far as how able you (and your colleagues) are in keeping this secret.

But let us take from this the insight that a malicious user needs to know which hash function is being used in order to purposefully generate large numbers of collisions. Rather than keep the hash function a secret, we simply use a set of hash functions, and allow our algorithm to pick randomly which one to actually use, without making its choice public. To 'normal' users, the hash table behaves exactly as expected, regardless of which hash function is used. In other words, the interface of the hash table has not changed. But even if a malicious user knows the whole set of hash functions, she does not know which one is actually being used by the hash table, and in principle cannot determine how to generate collisions.

Of course, if we picked a poor set of hash functions, it might be possible that each one has a huge number of collisions, or that the same keys collide for all or most of the functions. So we certainly need some restriction on the hash functions that can go into this set; we make this idea precise in the following definition.

dense_only.question: Compare closed addressing and open addressing for collision resolution.
dense_only.ground_truth: Closed addressing stores multiple items per table position using buckets or chains. Open addressing stores all items directly in the table and probes for another slot when collisions occur.
dense_only.answer:
Closed addressing and open addressing are two common techniques for collision resolution in hash tables:

- **Closed Addressing (Chaining):** Each bucket in the hash table contains a pointer to a linked list (or another data structure) of all elements whose keys hash to that bucket. Colliding keys are stored outside the main array in linked structures, allowing multiple keys to share the same hash index without searching for alternative locations.

- **Open Addressing:** All elements are stored directly in the hash table array itself. When a collision occurs, open addressing probes other positions in the table (using techniques like linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing) to find an empty slot. Keys are inserted into or searched by traversing these probe sequences.

Specifically, with open addressing, the probe sequence determines the order of array indices checked. For double hashing, the number of possible probe sequences is about m² (where m is the table size), making clustering less likely compared to linear or quadratic probing, which have at most m different probe sequences. This leads to better distribution and fewer collisions in double hashing [Source 2].

In summary, the main difference is that closed addressing uses linked structures to handle collisions, keeping keys at their hashed index but allowing multiple entries there, while open addressing resolves collisions by searching for other empty slots in the array according to a probe sequence.

dense_only.question: Why does load factor matter in hash table performance?
dense_only.ground_truth: The load factor measures how full the table is. Higher load factors generally increase collisions or probe lengths, hurting expected operation time.
dense_only.answer:
The load factor of a hash table, defined as the ratio of the number of keys stored (n) to the size of the table (m), denoted as \( \alpha = \frac{n}{m} \), directly impacts hash table performance because it reflects how full the table is and influences the average-case running time of operations like search and delete.

When the load factor is high, meaning the table is more full, the average number of probes or steps needed to find an item or an empty spot increases. For example, in closed addressing (chaining), the average-case running time of search and delete is proportional to \( O(1 + \alpha) \), because the keys mapping to the same bucket are stored in a list whose length grows with the load factor [Source 2].

In open addressing schemes, where each array element contains only one key and collisions are resolved by probing other indices, the load factor must be less than 1 to avoid an infinite loop when inserting new keys. The average number of indices examined in successful or unsuccessful searches depends on \( \frac{1}{1 - \alpha} \), which grows rapidly as the load factor approaches 1. For instance, at a load factor of 0.9, about 10 indices might be checked on average, which is still manageable, but performance degrades as the table nears full capacity [Source 3, Source 8].

Therefore, maintaining an appropriate load factor is crucial to ensure efficient hashing operations and avoid excessive collisions or probing, which degrade performance.

dense_only.question: Why does randomized quicksort avoid consistently bad pivot choices on fixed adversarial inputs?
dense_only.ground_truth: Randomizing the pivot makes the pivot choice independent of the input order, so no fixed input arrangement reliably causes the worst-case split pattern.
dense_only.answer:
Randomized quicksort avoids consistently bad pivot choices on fixed adversarial inputs by moving the randomness inside the algorithm, rather than relying on randomness in the input. Specifically, before running the deterministic quicksort, it randomly permutes the input array so that the pivot is effectively chosen from a random permutation of the elements. This random permutation makes every pivot equally likely to be any element of the array, preventing an adversary from constructing an input that always leads to worst-case partitions.

Because the random permutation hides any structure or ordering in the input, the algorithm cannot be forced to pick poor pivots systematically. Even if the adversary provides an input that is "bad" for the deterministic quicksort (like a sorted list), once permuted randomly, the pivot choices become essentially random, resulting in expected balanced partitions. Therefore, the expected running time over the algorithm’s internal randomness is always \( \Theta(n \log n) \), regardless of the input chosen by an adversary.

This means that while specific runs of randomized quicksort might still occasionally take longer, the average running time over multiple runs on the same input remains \( \Theta(n \log n) \), and the adversary cannot force the algorithm into its worst-case \( \Theta(n^2) \) behavior consistently [Source 1, Source 3, Source 7].

dense_only.question: What problem is universal hashing designed to reduce?
dense_only.ground_truth: Universal hashing reduces the chance that a fixed set of keys causes many collisions by randomly choosing a hash function from a family with good collision guarantees.
dense_only.answer:
Universal hashing is designed to reduce the problem of worst-case collisions that can occur when a fixed hash function is used. Specifically, if a single hash function is chosen and known, a malicious user could study this hash function and generate a set of keys that all hash to the same index, causing operations like search to degrade to linear time in the number of keys colliding at that index [Source 2, 7].

Universal hashing addresses this by selecting the hash function randomly from a carefully chosen set of hash functions known as a universal hash family. This randomization makes it impossible for a user to deliberately cause collisions in a predictable way because they do not know which hash function from the family is actually being used. Thus, universal hashing reduces the likelihood of collisions and ensures that the worst-case expected running time for operations like search remains efficient (O(1 + α), where α is the load factor) regardless of the key distribution [Sources 1, 3, 7].

6 Graphs

In this chapter, we will study the graph abstract data type, which is one of the most versatile and fundamental in computer science. You have already studied trees, which can be used to model hierarchical data like members of a family or a classification of living things. Graphs are a generalization of trees that can represent arbitrary (binary) relationships between various objects. Some common examples of graphs in practice are modelling geographic and spatial relationships; activity between members of a social network; requirements and dependencies in a complex system like the development of a space shuttle. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to define the graph ADT and compare different implementations of this data type; and perform and analyse algorithms which traverse graphs.

7 Amortized Analysis

In this chapter, we will study another form of algorithm analysis that offers a new type of refinement of worst-case analysis. To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

To cause this worst-case behaviour in practice, a malicious user would study the hash function used and determine such a set of colliding keys. You might be tempted, then, to keep your hash function a secret so that no one can figure out these collisions. But a reliance on such an approach only goes so far as how able you (and your colleagues) are in keeping this secret.

But let us take from this the insight that a malicious user needs to know which hash function is being used in order to purposefully generate large numbers of collisions. Rather than keep the hash function a secret, we simply use a set of hash functions, and allow our algorithm to pick randomly which one to actually use, without making its choice public. To 'normal' users, the hash table behaves exactly as expected, regardless of which hash function is used. In other words, the interface of the hash table has not changed. But even if a malicious user knows the whole set of hash functions, she does not know which one is actually being used by the hash table, and in principle cannot determine how to generate collisions.

Of course, if we picked a poor set of hash functions, it might be possible that each one has a huge number of collisions, or that the same keys collide for all or most of the functions. So we certainly need some restriction on the hash functions that can go into this set; we make this idea precise in the following definition.

To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

One can get around this problem by storing the hash table with a data structure that uses dynamically-allocated memory like a linked list or AVL tree, but then we lose the constant-time addressing feature that we get from storing items in a contiguous block of memory. In this chapter, we will study a variant of arrays called dynamic arrays , which we use to implement a resizable collection of items that supports constant-time addressing and 'efficient' insertion of new items. We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

Dynamic arrays

dense_only.question: Compare breadth-first search and depth-first search.
dense_only.ground_truth: BFS explores vertices by increasing distance from the start and is useful for shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS explores deeply before backtracking and is useful for structure discovery such as components or ordering.
dense_only.answer:
Breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS) are two fundamental graph traversal algorithms with different strategies and characteristics:

**Breadth-First Search (BFS):**  
- BFS starts at a given vertex and explores all of its neighbors first, then the neighbors of those neighbors, and so forth. This means it visits vertices in order of their distance from the starting vertex, exploring the graph in "layers" [Source 7].  
- BFS uses a queue data structure to keep track of vertices to visit next, which ensures that all vertices at distance \( d \) from the start are visited before any vertex at distance \( d+1 \) [Source 8].  
- BFS can be adapted to find the shortest path between two vertices in an unweighted graph by storing the parent of each vertex during traversal and reconstructing the path [Source 1].  
- BFS guarantees that if a vertex \( w \) is reachable from the start vertex \( v \), \( w \) will be visited after all vertices at smaller distances, confirming correctness [Source 5].  
- Its worst-case runtime is \( \Theta(|V| + |E|) \), where \( |V| \) and \( |E| \) are the number of vertices and edges, respectively [Source 2].

**Depth-First Search (DFS):**  
- DFS starts at a given vertex and explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. It visits a vertex’s neighbor recursively before moving to other neighbors, which dives deep into the graph paths [Source 4, 6].  
- DFS uses recursion and the function call stack (or an explicit stack) to handle backtracking when no unvisited neighbors remain [Source 6].  
- DFS marks vertices with "started" and "finished" states to track visitation status during the recursion, which helps in various applications such as cycle detection [Source 3, 6].  
- DFS also runs in worst-case \( \Theta(|V| + |E|) \) time [Source 2].  
- Unlike BFS, DFS does not guarantee visiting vertices in order of distance from the start vertex, so it is less suitable for shortest path computations [Source 3, 5].

Graph traversals: breadth-first search

We are now ready to do our first real algorithm on graphs. Consider the central problem of exploring a graph by traversing its edges (rather than relying on direct access of references or array indices). For example, we might want to take a social network, and print out the names of everyone who is connected to a particular person. We would like to be able to start from a given vertex in a graph, and then visit its neighbours, the neighbours of its neighbours, etc. until we have visited every vertex that is connected to it. Moreover, we'd like to do so efficiently .

For the next two sections, we will study two approaches for performing such an exploration in a principled way. The first approach is called breadth-first search (BFS) . The basic idea is to take a starting vertex s , visit its neighbours, then visit the neighbours of its neighbours, then the neighbours of its neighbours of its neighbours, proceeding until all of the vertices have been explored. The trick is doing so without repeatedly visiting the same vertex. To formalize this in an algorithm, we need a way to keep track of which vertices have already been visited, and which vertex should be visited next.

This lemma gets its name from the real-life example of meeting people at a party. Suppose a bunch of people are at a party always shake hands when they meet someone new. After greetings are done, if you ask each person how many new people they met and add them up, the sum is equal to twice the number of handshakes that occurred.

If we assume that the graph is connected, then such an exploration visits every vertex in the graph.

dense_only.question: Compare adjacency lists and adjacency matrices.
dense_only.ground_truth: Adjacency lists are space-efficient for sparse graphs and efficient for iterating neighbors. Adjacency matrices use more space but allow constant-time edge existence checks.
dense_only.answer:
Adjacency lists and adjacency matrices are two common data structures for representing graphs, each with distinct characteristics in terms of implementation and space complexity:

1. **Adjacency Lists:**
   - Represented by storing, for each vertex, a list of references to its neighbours.
   - The graph stores an array (or other collection) of these vertices.
   - Checking adjacency involves looking up the vertex and searching through its neighbour list, which takes time proportional to the number of neighbours.
   - Space complexity is \( \Theta(|V| + |E|) \), where \(|V|\) is the number of vertices and \(|E|\) the number of edges. This is because the array stores all vertices plus references to each edge.
   - Efficient for sparse graphs where \( |E| \ll |V|^2 \).
   - The sum of all neighbours (references) across vertices equals twice the number of edges in undirected graphs due to the handshake lemma.

2. **Adjacency Matrices:**
   - Represented as a two-dimensional boolean array of size \(|V| \times |V|\), where the \(ij\)-th entry is true if there is an edge between vertex \(i\) and \(j\).
   - Checking adjacency is constant time \(O(1)\) since it is a direct lookup in the matrix.
   - Space complexity is \( \Theta(|V|^2) \) because it stores information for every possible pair of vertices, including non-edges.
   - Simple to implement due to direct edge representation.
   - Not space-efficient for sparse graphs but can be more suitable when the graph is dense.

In summary, adjacency lists are more space-efficient and suitable for sparse graphs, although adjacency checks may take longer, while adjacency matrices provide constant-time adjacency checks but at the cost of higher space usage, especially for sparse graphs [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 8].
contexts:
Adjacency matrices

The previous approach was vertex-focused: each vertex is represented as a separate entity in the program, with edges stored implicitly as the references in the adjacency lists. It is also possible to represent the edges directly in what we call an adjacency matrix . Suppose there are n vertices in some graph, each with a label between 0 and n -1. We use an n -byn two-dimensional boolean array, where the ij -entry of the array is true if there is an edge between vertex i and vertex j .

Using this approach, determining adjacency in a graph runs in constant time, since it is just an array lookup:

1 def CheckAdjacent(G, i, j): 2 return G.adjacency[i][j]

Implementation space usage

The adjacency matrix approach seems conceptually simpler and easier to implement than the adjacency list approach. However, it does have a relatively high space cost, since it must use computer memory to store not only the edges, but also the 'non-edges.' This representation must store a full | V | -by-| V | matrix, with a space cost of Q ( | V | 2 ) .

In the adjacency list implementation, the graph itself stores an array of size Q ( | V | ) , and each vertex stores its label and references to its neighbours. We cannot count the number of references for an individual vertex because that can vary dramatically among vertices in an individual graph. But we do have a nice way of calculating the total number of references stored across all vertices.

Adjacency lists

The first approach is one that should be familiar, because it is essentially what we do to implement trees. We use a vertex data type that has a label attribute to identify the vertex, and a list of references to its neighbours. This latter attribute is known as an adjacency list , from which this implementation gets its name. Since the vertices keep track of the edge data, a second graph data type stores only a collection the vertices in the graph. To illustrate this approach, we show how one could implement a function that checks whether two vertices in a graph are adjacent. Note that this operation takes labels , and must use them to look up the corresponding vertices in the graph.

1 def CheckAdjacent(G, i, j): 2 # Access the vertices attribute and perform lookup by labels 3 u = G.vertices[i] 4 v = G.vertices[j] 5 for vertex in u.neighbours: 6 # Note: this assumes labels are unique 7 if vertex.label == v.label: 8 return True 9 10 return False

What is the running time of this algorithm? We assume that looking up the two vertices in graph.vertices takes constant time, so the running In our default undirected case, this means that two adjacent vertices each store a reference to the other in their respective adjacency lists.

A common implementation stores the vertices in an array, and labels each vertex with its array index. If we need to support arbitrary unique identifiers, any dictionary implementation (e.g., a hash table) can be used as well.

So this means the total cost of storing the references in our adjacency list data structure is Q ( | E | ) , for a total space cost of Q ( | V | + | E | ) (adding a | V | term for storing the labels). Note that this is the cost for storing all the vertices, not just a single vertex. Adding up the cost for the graph data structure and all the vertices gives a total space cost of Q ( | V | + | E | ) .

At first glance, it may seem that | V | 2 and | V | + | E | are incomparable. However, observe that the maximum number of possible edges is Q ( | V | 2 ) , which arises in the case when every vertex is adjacent to every other vertex. So in asymptotic terms, | V | + | E | = O ( | V | 2 ) , but this bound is not tight: if there are very few (e.g., O ( | V | ) ) edges then adjacency lists will be much more space efficient than the adjacency matrix.

dense_only.question: Why is DFS useful for identifying graph structure?
dense_only.ground_truth: DFS records discovery and finish behavior that reveals reachability, connected components, cycles, and ordering relationships in directed or undirected graphs.
dense_only.answer:
DFS (Depth-First Search) is useful for identifying graph structure because it systematically explores all vertices reachable from a starting vertex by prioritizing the exploration of as many vertices as possible before backtracking. This approach reveals connectivity, components, and the presence of cycles within the graph.

Specifically:

1. **Identification of Connected Components:** DFS visits every vertex connected to the starting vertex. Theorem 6.5 states that if a vertex \( w \) is connected to the starting vertex \( v \), DFS will visit \( w \). This helps identify which vertices belong to the same connected component in an undirected graph [Source 2].

2. **Tracking Discovery and Completion:** DFS assigns two attributes to each vertex—`started` (discovered but not fully explored) and `finished` (fully explored)—which capture the status of vertices during traversal. These attributes help understand the structure of the graph during exploration [Source 5].

3. **Cycle Detection:** DFS can be modified slightly to detect cycles efficiently. In an undirected graph, by tracking the parent of each vertex and checking if a started neighbor is not the parent, DFS can report the presence of a cycle. For directed graphs, checking neighbors that are started but not finished identifies cycles. This helps in recognizing redundancy and intricacies in the graph structure such as cyclic paths [Sources 1, 3, 4, 7].

4. **Understanding Reachability and Paths:** DFS helps determine paths and reachability since it explores vertices deeply along paths before backtracking. The search tree formed during DFS reveals the underlying structure of paths and connectivity [Source 2].

5. **Running Time Efficiency:** DFS runs efficiently in \( O(|V| + |E|) \) time, making it practical for analyzing the structure of large graphs [Sources 1, 2].

In summary, DFS provides insights into graph connectivity, cycles, and overall structure by virtue of its systematic exploration and status-tracking mechanism in an efficient manner.

References: [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7]

Started but not finished: has been visited by the search, but some vertices reachable from this vertex without revisiting other started vertices still need to be visited.

Started and finished: it has been visited by the search, and all vertices reachable from this vertex without revisiting other started vertices have been visited.

Cycles encode a natural 'redundancy' in a graph: it is possible to remove any edge in a cycle without disconnecting its vertices (just take the long way around the cycle), and so it is often useful to know whether a graph has a cycle, or whether it does not. It turns out that determining whether a graph has a cycle or not can be done through a simple modification of either breadth-first or depth-first search, though we will only show the DFS version here.

Recall that depth-first search sets two attributes started and finished for each vertex, which are used to track the status of the vertex in the search. Intuitively, we can use these to detect cycles by checking whether we have reached an already-visited node when performing a search. Below, we give a modified version of DFS that reports when it detects a cycle, with two main changes to the implementation:

That is, a cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex.

Each vertex other than the starting vertex stores its parent vertex, which is the neighbour that caused the vertex to be visited

The inner loop contains a check for started neighbours that are not the parent of the current vertex; as we'll show later, this is a valid check for a cycle.

The caveat for our (quite simple) implementation is that it only works when the graph is connected; we leave it as an exercise to decide how to modify it to always report a cycle, even when the graph is not connected.

You may notice that the finished attribute is not used by the algorithm itself; however, it does play a helpful role in analysing the behaviour of DFS. At any point during the run of DFS, each vertex has one of three possible states:

Not started: has not been visited by the search.

Started but not finished: has been visited by the search, but some vertices reachable from this vertex without revisiting other started vertices still need to be visited.

Started and finished: it has been visited by the search, and all vertices reachable from this vertex without revisiting other started vertices have been visited.

dense_only.question: What is a minimum spanning tree?
dense_only.ground_truth: A minimum spanning tree is a set of edges connecting all vertices of a connected weighted graph with no cycles and minimum total edge weight.
dense_only.answer: A minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected weighted graph \( G = (V, E) \) is a subset of edges \( E' \subseteq E \) such that the graph \( (V, E') \) is a tree (connected and has no cycles) that spans all the vertices, and the sum of the weights of the edges in \( E' \) is minimized. In other words, it connects all the vertices together with the minimum possible total edge weight [Source 1].

Definition 6 . 8 (tree) . A tree is a connected graph that has no cycles.

So you can view our goal as taking a connected graph, and identifying a subset of the edges to keep, which results in a tree on the vertices of the original graph.

It turns out that the unweighted case is not very interesting, because all trees obey a simple relationship between their number of edges and vertices: every tree with n vertices has exactly n -1 edges. So finding such a tree can be done quite easily by repeatedly finding cycles and choosing to keep all but one of the edges.

However, the weighted case is more challenging, and is the problem of study in this section.

Definition 6 . 9 (minimum spanning tree) . The Minimum Spanning Tree Problem takes as input a connected weighted graph G = ( V , E ) , and outputs a set of edges E ′ such that the graph ( V , E ′ ) is a tree, and which minimizes the sum of the weights e ∈ E ′ we . We call such the resulting tree

a minimum spanning tree (MST) of G .

Prim's algorithm

The first algorithm we will study for solving this problem is known as Prim's algorithm . The basic idea of this algorithm is quite straightforward: pick a starting vertex for the tree, and then repeatedly add new vertices to the tree, each time selecting an edge with minimum weight that connects the current tree to a new vertex.

We won't prove this here, but please take a course on graph theory if you interested in exploring more properties like this in greater detail.

Warning: one difference between this definition of tree and the trees you are used to seeing as data structures is that the latter are rooted, meaning we give one vertex special status as the root of the tree. This is not the case for trees in general.

As with shortest paths, there might be more than one minimum spanning tree of G . We just want to find one.

1 def PrimMST(G): 2 v = pick starting vertex from G.vertices 3 TV = {v} # MST vertices 4 TE = {} # MST edges 5 6 while TV != G.vertices: 7 extensions = { (u, v) in G.edges where exactly one of u, v are in TV } 8 e = edge in extensions having minimum weight 9 TV = TV + endpoints of e 10 TE = TE + {e} 11 12 return TE

This algorithm is quite remarkable for two reasons. The first is that it works regardless of which starting vertex is chosen; in other words, there is no such thing as the 'best' starting vertex for this algorithm. The second is that it works without ever backtracking and discarding an already-selected edge to choose a different one. Let us spend some time studying the algorithm to prove that it is indeed correct.

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Kruskal's algorithm

As a bridge between this chapter and our next major topic of discussion, we will look at another algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem. You might wonder why we need another algorithm at all: didn't we just spend a lot of time developing an algorithm that seems to work perfectly well? But of course, there are plenty of reasons to study more than one algorithm for solving a given problem, much as there is for studying more than one implementation of a given ADT: generation of new ideas or insights into problem structure; improving running time efficiency; different possible directions of generalization. In this particular case, we have a pedagogical reason for introducing this algorithm here as well, as motivation for the final abstract data type we will study in this course.

The second algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem is known as Kruskal's algorithm . It is quite similar to Prim's algorithm, in that it incrementally builds up an MST by selecting 'good' edges one Exercise: why is each edge added at most once?

at a time. Rather than build up a single connected component of vertices, however, it simply sorts edges by weight, and always picks the smallestweight edge that doesn't create a cycle with the edges already selected.

1 def KruskalMST(G): 2 TE = {} 3 sort G.edges in non-decreasing order of weights 4 5 for e in G.edges: # starting with the smallest weight edge 6 if TE + {e} does not have a cycle: 7 TE = TE + {e} 8 9 return TE

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Proof. The proof of correctness of Prim's algorithm is an interesting one, because it relies on two loop invariants, one of which is straightforward, but the other of which is very neat and unexpected if you haven't seen anything like it before. Here are our two invariants (remember that these are true at the beginning and end of every iteration of the loop):

( 1 ) The graph ( TV , TE ) is a tree.

( 2 ) The tree ( TV , TE ) can be extended by only adding some edges and vertices to a minimum spanning tree of G .

Before we prove that these invariants are correct, let's see why they imply the correctness of Prim's algorithm. When the loop terminates, both of these invariants hold, so the graph ( TV , TE ) is a tree and can be extended to an MST for the input graph. However, when the loop terminates, its condition is false, and so TV contains all the vertices in the graph. This means that ( TV , TE ) must be an MST for the input graph, since no more vertices/edges can be added to extend it into one.

This is actually where the choice of data structures is important. Note that we have two sets here, a set of vertices and a set of edges. We'll first use an array to represent these sets, so looking up a particular item or adding a new item takes constant time.

How do we compute extensions , the edges that have one endpoint in TV and one endpoint not in TV ? We can loop through all the edges, each time checking its endpoints; this takes Q ( m ) time. What about computing the minimum weight edge? This is linear in the size of extensions , and so in the worst case is Q ( m ) .

This leads to a total running time of Q ( mn ) , which is not great (recall that BFS and DFS both took time linear in the two quantities, Q ( n + m ) ). The key inefficiency here is that the inner computations of finding 'extension' edges and finding the minimum weight edge both do a lot of repeated work in different iterations of the outer loop. After all, from one iteration to the next, the extensions only change slightly, since the set TV only changes by one vertex.

However, there is a much smarter way of checking whether adding a given edge creates a cycle or not, by keeping track of the connected components of the vertices defined by the edges in TE . At the beginning of Kruskal's algorithm, we can view each vertex as being its own component, since TE is empty. When the first edge is added, its two endpoints are merged into the same component. As more and more edges are added, components merge together, until eventually there is only one component, the minimum spanning tree.

How does this help us check whether adding an edge creates a cycle or not? We look at the two endpoints of the new edge: if they are in the same connected component, then adding the edge creates a cycle; otherwise, adding an edge doesn't create a cycle, and causes the two components of its endpoints to be merged.

Well, this is at least the obvious upper bound calculation. We leave it as an exercise to prove a tight lower bound on the worst-case running time.

The running time of the algorithm now depends on how quickly we can maintain these components while performing these three operations:

create a new component for each vertex

determine whether two vertices are in the same component

merge two components together

dense_only.ground_truth: Prim's algorithm grows one tree by repeatedly adding a cheapest edge from the tree to a new vertex. Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges and adds safe edges that connect different components.
dense_only.answer:
Prim's algorithm and Kruskal's algorithm are both classical methods to find a minimum spanning tree (MST) in a connected, weighted graph, but they differ significantly in approach and implementation details:

**Prim's algorithm:**
- Starts from an arbitrary vertex and grows the MST by repeatedly adding the minimum weight edge that connects a vertex in the MST to a vertex outside it.
- Maintains a set of included vertices \( TV \) and edges \( TE \).
- At each step, it finds edges that connect \( TV \) to remaining vertices and picks the minimum weight edge among them.
- It does not backtrack or discard edges once selected.
- The correctness is based on invariants that ensure at each step \( (TV, TE) \) is a tree extendable to an MST.
- The naive implementation can have a running time of \( O(nm) \), where \( n \) is vertices and \( m \) is edges, because finding the minimum edge in each iteration can involve checking all edges.
- The choice of the initial vertex does not affect the final MST produced.

**Kruskal's algorithm:**
- Starts with all vertices as individual components.
- Sorts all edges by weight.
- Iteratively adds the smallest weight edge that does not form a cycle with previously added edges.
- Uses a data structure to keep track of connected components (e.g., union-find) to efficiently determine if adding an edge creates a cycle.
- The main cost is sorting edges \( O(m \log m) \).
- Checking for cycles is efficient with union-find operations for component merges and queries.
- The algorithm ends when it connects all components into a single MST.
- Its simplicity contrasts with Prim's approach of growing a single connected component.

**Summary comparison:**
- Prim builds the MST by growing a single subtree and adding the minimal connecting edge at each step.
- Kruskal builds the MST by considering edges globally in increasing order, adding only those edges that keep the graph acyclic.
- Prim's algorithm is vertex-based, Kruskal's is edge-based.
- Prim can be more efficient for dense graphs using appropriate data structures (priority queues), while Kruskal can outperform on sparse graphs due to edge sorting and union-find.
- Both guarantee correctness and output a minimum spanning tree.

These points illustrate why both algorithms are important: to provide different perspectives, efficiencies, and insights into the MST problem and related data structures [Sources 1,

Definition 6 . 8 (tree) . A tree is a connected graph that has no cycles.

So you can view our goal as taking a connected graph, and identifying a subset of the edges to keep, which results in a tree on the vertices of the original graph.

It turns out that the unweighted case is not very interesting, because all trees obey a simple relationship between their number of edges and vertices: every tree with n vertices has exactly n -1 edges. So finding such a tree can be done quite easily by repeatedly finding cycles and choosing to keep all but one of the edges.

However, the weighted case is more challenging, and is the problem of study in this section.

Definition 6 . 9 (minimum spanning tree) . The Minimum Spanning Tree Problem takes as input a connected weighted graph G = ( V , E ) , and outputs a set of edges E ′ such that the graph ( V , E ′ ) is a tree, and which minimizes the sum of the weights e ∈ E ′ we . We call such the resulting tree

a minimum spanning tree (MST) of G .

Prim's algorithm

The first algorithm we will study for solving this problem is known as Prim's algorithm . The basic idea of this algorithm is quite straightforward: pick a starting vertex for the tree, and then repeatedly add new vertices to the tree, each time selecting an edge with minimum weight that connects the current tree to a new vertex.

We won't prove this here, but please take a course on graph theory if you interested in exploring more properties like this in greater detail.

Kruskal's algorithm

As a bridge between this chapter and our next major topic of discussion, we will look at another algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem. You might wonder why we need another algorithm at all: didn't we just spend a lot of time developing an algorithm that seems to work perfectly well? But of course, there are plenty of reasons to study more than one algorithm for solving a given problem, much as there is for studying more than one implementation of a given ADT: generation of new ideas or insights into problem structure; improving running time efficiency; different possible directions of generalization. In this particular case, we have a pedagogical reason for introducing this algorithm here as well, as motivation for the final abstract data type we will study in this course.

The second algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem is known as Kruskal's algorithm . It is quite similar to Prim's algorithm, in that it incrementally builds up an MST by selecting 'good' edges one Exercise: why is each edge added at most once?

at a time. Rather than build up a single connected component of vertices, however, it simply sorts edges by weight, and always picks the smallestweight edge that doesn't create a cycle with the edges already selected.

1 def KruskalMST(G): 2 TE = {} 3 sort G.edges in non-decreasing order of weights 4 5 for e in G.edges: # starting with the smallest weight edge 6 if TE + {e} does not have a cycle: 7 TE = TE + {e} 8 9 return TE

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Proof. The proof of correctness of Prim's algorithm is an interesting one, because it relies on two loop invariants, one of which is straightforward, but the other of which is very neat and unexpected if you haven't seen anything like it before. Here are our two invariants (remember that these are true at the beginning and end of every iteration of the loop):

( 1 ) The graph ( TV , TE ) is a tree.

( 2 ) The tree ( TV , TE ) can be extended by only adding some edges and vertices to a minimum spanning tree of G .

Before we prove that these invariants are correct, let's see why they imply the correctness of Prim's algorithm. When the loop terminates, both of these invariants hold, so the graph ( TV , TE ) is a tree and can be extended to an MST for the input graph. However, when the loop terminates, its condition is false, and so TV contains all the vertices in the graph. This means that ( TV , TE ) must be an MST for the input graph, since no more vertices/edges can be added to extend it into one.

We will omit the proof of the first invariant, which is rather straightforward. The second one is significantly more interesting, and harder to This algorithm doesn't 'make mistakes' when choosing edges.

Remember: trees are connected and have no cycles.

We won't prove this here, but please take a course on graph theory if you interested in exploring more properties like this in greater detail.

Warning: one difference between this definition of tree and the trees you are used to seeing as data structures is that the latter are rooted, meaning we give one vertex special status as the root of the tree. This is not the case for trees in general.

As with shortest paths, there might be more than one minimum spanning tree of G . We just want to find one.

1 def PrimMST(G): 2 v = pick starting vertex from G.vertices 3 TV = {v} # MST vertices 4 TE = {} # MST edges 5 6 while TV != G.vertices: 7 extensions = { (u, v) in G.edges where exactly one of u, v are in TV } 8 e = edge in extensions having minimum weight 9 TV = TV + endpoints of e 10 TE = TE + {e} 11 12 return TE

This algorithm is quite remarkable for two reasons. The first is that it works regardless of which starting vertex is chosen; in other words, there is no such thing as the 'best' starting vertex for this algorithm. The second is that it works without ever backtracking and discarding an already-selected edge to choose a different one. Let us spend some time studying the algorithm to prove that it is indeed correct.

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Nowdefine the edge set E ′′ to be the same as E ′ , except with e ′ removed and e added. The resulting graph ( V , E ′′ ) is still connected, and doesn't contain any cycles - it is a tree. Moreover, the total weight of its edges is less than or equal to that of E ′ , since we ′ ≥ we . Then the graph ( V , E ′′ ) is also a minimum spanning tree of the input graph, and E ⊆ E ′′ .

The idea of replacing e ′ by e in the initial MST to form a new MST is a very nice one. Intuitively, we argued that at the loop iteration where we 'should' have chosen e ′ to go into the MST, choosing e instead was still just as good, and also leads to a correct solution. It is precisely this argument, 'every choice leads to a correct solution', that allows Prim's algorithm to never backtrack, undoing a choice to make a different one. This has significant efficiency implications, as we'll study in the next section.

Analysis of Prim's algorithm

What is the running time of Prim's algorithm? Let n be the number of vertices in the graph, and m be the number of edges. We know that the outer loop always runs exactly n times. Each iteration adds one new vertex to the set TV ; the loop terminates only when TV contains all n vertices. But This assumption is precisely the loop invariant being true at the beginning of the loop body.

Note that their weights could be equal.

1 def KruskalMST(G): 2 TE = {} 3 sort G.edges in non-decreasing order of weights 4 5 for e in G.edges: # starting with the smallest weight edge 6 if TE + {e} does not have a cycle: 7 TE = TE + {e} 8 9 return TE

We will omit the proof of correctness of Kruskal's algorithm, although it is quite remarkable that this algorithm works correctly given its simplicity.

The running time of this algorithm is more interesting. The sorting of edges takes Q ( | E | log | E | ) in the worst-case and the outer loop runs at most | E | times. The really interesting part of the algorithm comes from checking whether adding a new edge e to TE creates a cycle or not. A natural approach is to use what we learned earlier in this chapter and perform either a depth-first or breadth-first search starting from one of the endpoints of the chosen edge, using only the edges in TE + {e} . This is rather inefficient, since the O ( | V | + | E | ) running time of the search is repeated O ( | E | ) times, for a total running time of O ( | E | log | E | + | E | ( | V | + | E | )) = O ( | E | · | V | + | E | 2 ) .

However, there is a much smarter way of checking whether adding a given edge creates a cycle or not, by keeping track of the connected components of the vertices defined by the edges in TE . At the beginning of Kruskal's algorithm, we can view each vertex as being its own component, since TE is empty. When the first edge is added, its two endpoints are merged into the same component. As more and more edges are added, components merge together, until eventually there is only one component, the minimum spanning tree.

How does this help us check whether adding an edge creates a cycle or not? We look at the two endpoints of the new edge: if they are in the same connected component, then adding the edge creates a cycle; otherwise, adding an edge doesn't create a cycle, and causes the two components of its endpoints to be merged.

Well, this is at least the obvious upper bound calculation. We leave it as an exercise to prove a tight lower bound on the worst-case running time.

1 def KruskalMST(G): 2 TE = {} 3 sort G.edges in non-decreasing order of weights 4 set each vertex to be its own connected component 5 6 for e in G.edges: # starting with the smallest weight edge 7 if the endpoints of e are not in the same connected component: 8 TE = TE + {e} 9 merge the connected components containing the endpoints of e 10 11 return TE

The running time of the algorithm now depends on how quickly we can maintain these components while performing these three operations:

create a new component for each vertex

determine whether two vertices are in the same component

merge two components together

Note that their weights could be equal.

In fact, because E ′ forms a minimum spanning tree, the total weight of E ′′ can't be smaller than E ′ , so their weights are equal.

what happens inside the loop body?

This is actually where the choice of data structures is important. Note that we have two sets here, a set of vertices and a set of edges. We'll first use an array to represent these sets, so looking up a particular item or adding a new item takes constant time.

How do we compute extensions , the edges that have one endpoint in TV and one endpoint not in TV ? We can loop through all the edges, each time checking its endpoints; this takes Q ( m ) time. What about computing the minimum weight edge? This is linear in the size of extensions , and so in the worst case is Q ( m ) .

This leads to a total running time of Q ( mn ) , which is not great (recall that BFS and DFS both took time linear in the two quantities, Q ( n + m ) ). The key inefficiency here is that the inner computations of finding 'extension' edges and finding the minimum weight edge both do a lot of repeated work in different iterations of the outer loop. After all, from one iteration to the next, the extensions only change slightly, since the set TV only changes by one vertex.

dense_only.question: Why does appending to a dynamic array have constant amortized time even though resizing is expensive?
dense_only.ground_truth: Resizing happens only occasionally. The high cost of copying during a resize is spread over many cheap append operations, yielding constant average cost per append over a sequence.
dense_only.answer:
Appending to a dynamic array has constant amortized time despite occasional expensive resizings because the costly resizing operations happen infrequently and are compensated by many cheap insertions.

Here is the detailed explanation:

1. **Expensive resizing is rare:** A resizing (expansion) occurs only when the array is full, which happens when the number of elements reaches a power of two (e.g., 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...). When resizing occurs, the entire array is copied to a new larger array, which takes O(n) time for n elements.

2. **Many cheap insertions occur between resizes:** Before reaching a full array requiring resizing, you perform many insertions that each take only O(1) time. For example, after resizing an array to length 1024, there must have been 511 very fast insertions into the array that don't trigger resizing and thus take constant-time array accesses [Source 2].

3. **Amortized analysis perspective:** Instead of analyzing one operation in isolation (worst case), amortized analysis considers the total cost of a sequence of M insertions. Although some insertions are expensive (cause resizing), most are cheap. When the total cost of all M insertions is divided by M, the average cost per insertion becomes constant, O(1) [Source 1 and 3].

4. **Aggregate method:** Summing the costs of all insertions shows that the total runtime grows linearly with the number of insertions M, meaning the average or amortized cost per insertion is a constant — between 3 and 5 array accesses approximately [Source 3 and 6].

5. **Accounting method:** Alternatively, by charging each insertion a fixed cost (like 5 credits), the excess charge from cheap insertions accumulates to pay for the expensive resizing operations later. This scheme ensures that the amortized cost assigned to each insertion operation is constant, as the few costly resizings are balanced by the many cheap insertions [Source 7 and 8].

**Summary:** The expensive resizing happens sparsely and is "paid for" by the frequent constant-time insertions between resizes. This balancing act results in constant amortized time for appending elements to a dynamic array.

Hence, appending to a dynamic array has O(1) amortized running time, even though some individual insertions may cost O(n) due to resizing [Sources 1–

So we can contextualize the 'inefficient' insertion into the full 1024 -length array by noting that it must have been preceded by 511 extremely efficient insertions, which doesn't sound so bad.

More formally, an amortized analysis of a data structure computes the maximum possible average cost per operation in a sequence of operations , starting from some initial base state. Unlike both worst- and average-case analyses, we are not concerned here with studying one individual operation, but rather the total cost of a sequence of operations performed on a data structure, and relating this to the number of operations performed. There are two different ways of thinking about the amortized cost of a set of Remember that the expansion is caused when a new item is inserted, so the expanded array starts with 513 elements in it.

You can ignore the 'maximum possible' for now, since for dynamic arrays we only have one possible operation -insertion - and hence one possible sequence of operations.

operations:

The average cost of an operation when multiple operations are performed in a row. Note that this is a different use of 'average' than average-case analysis, which considers an operation as an isolated event, but allows for consideration of multiple inputs .

The total cost of a sequence of M operations as a function of M . Note that a sequence of M constant-time operations must have a total running time of Q ( M ) , so expressions that look 'linear' aren't directly referencing the worst-case running time of a single operation, but rather the rate of growth of the runtime of the entire sequence.

Aggregate method

Before we give a formal definition of amortized analysis, let us expand on one important detail from our informal discussion in the previous section. We observed that dynamic array insertion was only very rarely slow (when the number of items is a power of two, meaning that the array is full), with any other insertion being extremely fast. But even more is true: the only way to reach the 'bad' state of inserting into a full array is by first performing a series of (mostly fast) insertions.

Consider inserting an item into a full array of allocated length 2 10 = 1024. Since 1024 is a power of two, we know that this will take 2049 array accesses. However, to even reach such a state, we must have first taken an array of length 512 , expanded it to an array of length 1024 , and then performed 511 insertions to fill up the expanded array. And these 511 insertions would each have taken just one array access each!

So we can contextualize the 'inefficient' insertion into the full 1024 -length array by noting that it must have been preceded by 511 extremely efficient insertions, which doesn't sound so bad.

The last term there looks a little intimidating, but note that the floor doesn't change the value of the exponent much, and that the power and the log roughly cancel each other out:

So the total cost is between roughly 3 m and 5 m . This might sound linear, but remember that we are considering a sequence of M operations, and so the key point is that the average cost per operation in a sequence is actually between 3 and 5 , which is constant! So we conclude that the amortized cost of dynamic array insertion is Q ( 1 ) , formalizing our earlier intuition that the inefficient insertions are balanced out by the much more frequent fast insertions.

Accounting (banker's) method

Nowlet us perform the analysis again through a different technique known as the accounting method , also known as the banker's method . As before, our setup is to consider a sequence of M insertion operations on our dynamic array. In this approach, we do not try to compute the total cost of these insertions directly, but instead associate with each operation a charge , which is simply a positive number, with the property that the total value of the M charges is greater than or equal to the total cost of the M operations .

You may find it strange that the key variable is the number of operations, not the size of the data structure like usual. In amortized analysis, the size of the data structure is usually tied implicitly to the number of operations performed.

Worst-case running time of dynamic arrays

For the purposes of analysing the running time of this data structure, we will only count the number of array accesses made. This actually allows us to compute an exact number for the cost, which will be useful in the following sections.

For now, suppose we have a dynamic array where all n allocated spots are full. We note that the final two steps involve just one array access (inserting the new item x ), while the code executed in the if block has exactly 2 n accesses: accessing each of the n items in the old array and copying each item to the new array.

So we have a worst-case running time of 2 n + 1 = O ( n ) array accesses. This upper bound does not seem very impressive: AVL trees were able to support insertion in worst-case Q ( log n ) time, for instance. So why should we bother with dynamic arrays at all? Dynamic arrays

The idea of a dynamic array is to keep the fundamental array property of storing items in a contiguous memory block, but allow the array to expand when the existing array is full. dense_only.original_query: Why does appending to a dynamic array have constant amortized time even though resizing is expensive?

The answer is clear, detailed, and pedagogically useful.

dense_only.question: Compare aggregate, accounting, and potential methods in amortized analysis.
dense_only.ground_truth: The aggregate method bounds the total cost of a sequence directly. The accounting method assigns artificial charges to operations. The potential method uses a stored potential function to represent prepaid work.
dense_only.answer:
In amortized analysis, the aggregate, accounting (banker's), and potential methods are three different techniques used to analyze the average cost of a sequence of operations in a data structure.

1. **Aggregate Method**  
   - This method calculates the total cost of a sequence of \( M \) operations and then divides this total by \( M \) to find the average cost per operation.  
   - It is straightforward: first sum the costs over the sequence, then average to get the amortized cost per operation.  
   - For example, consider insertions into a dynamic array. The total cost includes frequent cheap insertions and rare expensive expansions. By adding these costs over all insertions, the aggregate method shows that the amortized cost per insertion is constant, \( O(1) \) [Source 6].  
   - It is simple but does not provide insight into the cost of individual operations.

2. **Accounting (Banker's) Method**  
   - This is a more flexible but challenging method that associates a fixed "charge" or "credit" with each operation. The charge is often more than the actual cost of some operations, "saving" credits that pay for future costly operations.  
   - The main idea is to assign charges so that the total amount charged over the sequence covers the actual total cost.  
   - Crucially, the method tracks "credits" conceptually—these credits are not part of the data structure but are an analytical tool to ensure that the total charge always exceeds total cost.  
   - For example, in dynamic arrays, the charge can be set to 5 credits per insertion operation; some of these cover the immediate cost, while others accumulate to pay for costly array resizes later. This approach also leads to an amortized cost of \( O(1) \) per insertion [Sources 1, 3, 4].  
   - It can handle sequences where individual operations vary greatly in cost.

3. **Potential Method** (Not explicitly detailed in the provided sources but commonly known in amortized analysis)  
   - Although not directly described in the sources, the potential method uses a potential function that maps the state of a data structure to a numeric value ("potential").  
   - The amortized cost of an operation is defined as the actual cost plus the change in potential, capturing the "stored work" in the structure.

dense_only.question: Why does union by rank help tree-based disjoint sets?
dense_only.ground_truth: Union by rank attaches the shallower or lower-rank tree under the higher-rank tree, limiting height growth and making future finds faster.
dense_only.answer:
Union by rank helps tree-based disjoint sets by enforcing a local property on the nodes that tends to keep the trees roughly balanced. Instead of arbitrarily choosing which tree root becomes the new root in a union, union by rank always makes the root with the larger rank the parent. The rank is defined recursively as the height of the tree (the rank of a leaf is 0, and the rank of an internal node is one plus the maximum rank of its children) and only increases when two roots have the same rank.

This heuristic prevents tall skinny trees because it always attaches the smaller (lower rank) tree below the larger (higher rank) tree, ensuring that the height of any tree grows slowly. Specifically, it is shown that the height of any tree is bounded by \(O(\log n)\), where \(n\) is the number of elements, so the worst-case time complexity for Find and Union operations improves from potentially linear \(Q(n)\) to \(Q(\log n)\) when using union by rank.

Thus, union by rank reduces the maximum height of trees in the disjoint set forest, which directly improves the efficiency of Find and Union operations by limiting the number of steps needed to reach the root during these operations [Source 1, Source 2, Source 3, Source 6, Source 7].
