hybrid.question: Why does load factor matter in hash table performance?
hybrid.ground_truth: The load factor measures how full the table is. Higher load factors generally increase collisions or probe lengths, hurting expected operation time.
hybrid.answer:
The load factor in a hash table matters because it directly affects the average-case running time of operations such as search and delete. The load factor, denoted as \( \alpha = \frac{n}{m} \), is the ratio of the number of keys stored (\(n\)) to the number of slots in the table (\(m\)).

When the load factor increases (meaning more keys per slot on average), the average number of items that need to be examined during search and deletion increases. Specifically, for hash tables with chaining (closed addressing), the average-case running time for Search and Delete operations is \(O(1 + \alpha)\). Thus, a higher load factor generally leads to slower operations because it implies longer linked lists or more keys per bucket to traverse.

In the case of open addressing (where each slot holds only one key and collisions are resolved by probing alternative slots), the load factor must always be less than 1 for the table to function properly. The average number of probes during searches is at most \(\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\), meaning as the load factor approaches 1, the number of probes grows significantly, reducing performance.

Hence, load factor is critical because it influences how many elements the hash table needs to inspect on average during key operations, directly impacting performance. Keeping the load factor low helps maintain efficient constant-time operations in hashing [Source 1, Source 3, Source 4].

On this path, you can see the cost of our traditional two-level page table: two additional memory accesses to look up a valid translation.

20.4 Inverted Page Tables

An even more extreme space savings in the world of page tables is found with inverted page tables . Here, instead of having many page tables (one per process of the system), we keep a single page table that has an entry for each physical page of the system. The entry tells us which process is using this page, and which virtual page of that process maps to this physical page.

Finding the correct entry is now a matter of searching through this data structure. A linear scan would be expensive, and thus a hash table is often built over the base structure to speed lookups. The PowerPC is one example of such an architecture [JM98].

More generally, inverted page tables illustrate what we've said from the beginning: page tables are just data structures. You can do lots of crazy things with data structures, making them smaller or bigger, making them slower or faster. Multi-level and inverted page tables are just two examples of the many things one could do.

20.5 Swapping the Page Tables to Disk

structure, we add a level of indirection through use of the page directory, which points to pieces of the page table; that indirection allows us to place page-table pages wherever we would like in physical memory.

It should be noted that there is a cost to multi-level tables; on a TLB miss, two loads from memory will be required to get the right translation information from the page table (one for the page directory, and one for the PTE itself), in contrast to just one load with a linear page table. Thus, the multi-level table is a small example of a time-space trade-off . We wanted smaller tables (and got them), but not for free; although in the common case (TLB hit), performance is obviously identical, a TLB miss suffers from a higher cost with this smaller table.

Another obvious negative is complexity . Whether it is the hardware or OS handling the page-table lookup (on a TLB miss), doing so is undoubtedly more involved than a simple linear page-table lookup. Often we are willing to increase complexity in order to improve performance or reduce overheads; in the case of a multi-level table, we make page-table lookups more complicated in order to save valuable memory.

On this path, you can see the cost of our traditional two-level page table: two additional memory accesses to look up a valid translation.

20.4 Inverted Page Tables

An even more extreme space savings in the world of page tables is found with inverted page tables . Here, instead of having many page tables (one per process of the system), we keep a single page table that has an entry for each physical page of the system. The entry tells us which process is using this page, and which virtual page of that process maps to this physical page.

Finding the correct entry is now a matter of searching through this data structure. A linear scan would be expensive, and thus a hash table is often built over the base structure to speed lookups. The PowerPC is one example of such an architecture [JM98].

More generally, inverted page tables illustrate what we've said from the beginning: page tables are just data structures. You can do lots of crazy things with data structures, making them smaller or bigger, making them slower or faster. Multi-level and inverted page tables are just two examples of the many things one could do.

structure, we add a level of indirection through use of the page directory, which points to pieces of the page table; that indirection allows us to place page-table pages wherever we would like in physical memory.

It should be noted that there is a cost to multi-level tables; on a TLB miss, two loads from memory will be required to get the right translation information from the page table (one for the page directory, and one for the PTE itself), in contrast to just one load with a linear page table. Thus, the multi-level table is a small example of a time-space trade-off . We wanted smaller tables (and got them), but not for free; although in the common case (TLB hit), performance is obviously identical, a TLB miss suffers from a higher cost with this smaller table.

Another obvious negative is complexity . Whether it is the hardware or OS handling the page-table lookup (on a TLB miss), doing so is undoubtedly more involved than a simple linear page-table lookup. Often we are willing to increase complexity in order to improve performance or reduce overheads; in the case of a multi-level table, we make page-table lookups more complicated in order to save valuable memory.

hybrid.question: Why does randomized quicksort avoid consistently bad pivot choices on fixed adversarial inputs?
hybrid.ground_truth: Randomizing the pivot makes the pivot choice independent of the input order, so no fixed input arrangement reliably causes the worst-case split pattern.
hybrid.answer:
Randomized quicksort avoids consistently bad pivot choices on fixed adversarial inputs by moving the randomness inside the algorithm itself. Instead of assuming the input is randomly ordered, the algorithm begins by applying a random permutation to the input list, effectively transforming any fixed input into a random one. This random permutation ensures that each element is equally likely to be chosen as the pivot in every recursive call, preventing an adversary from crafting an input that forces worst-case behavior.

As a result, even if an adversary chooses a "bad" input that would cause deterministic quicksort (which always picks the first element as pivot) to run in quadratic time, randomized quicksort maintains an expected running time of \( \mathcal{O}(n \log n) \) on that input because the pivot selections are randomized internally. Over many runs, the average running time remains efficient regardless of the input, as the adversary cannot predict or influence the randomized pivot choices made by the algorithm during execution [Source 1, Source 2, Source 4, Source 6].

In summary, randomized quicksort's internal random pivot selection breaks the correlation between fixed inputs and bad pivot choices, ensuring good expected performance on every input, including adversarial ones.

hybrid.question: What problem is universal hashing designed to reduce?
hybrid.ground_truth: Universal hashing reduces the chance that a fixed set of keys causes many collisions by randomly choosing a hash function from a family with good collision guarantees.
hybrid.answer:
Universal hashing is designed to reduce the problem of malicious or adversarial inputs causing worst-case behavior in hash tables. Specifically, if a fixed hash function is used, it is possible for an attacker who knows the function to select a set of keys that all collide (hash to the same index), resulting in degenerate search times of order \( \Theta(n) \). Universal hashing addresses this by randomly selecting a hash function from a universal family at the creation of the hash table, making it unlikely for an adversarial input to cause many collisions. This approach removes the reliance on keeping the hash function secret and ensures that the worst-case expected running time of search operations remains low regardless of input distribution [Source 1], [Source 3].

In summary, universal hashing reduces the likelihood and impact of collisions caused by an adversarial choice of keys, protecting against worst-case performance scenarios in hash table operations.

Our algorithm is now quite simple. When a new hash table is created, it picks a hash function uniformly at random from a universal hash family, and uses this to do its hashing. This type of hashing is called universal hashing , and is a randomized implementation of hashing commonly used in practice.

Analysis of universal hashing

Consider a universal hashing scheme that uses closed addressing (chaining). We will consider the worst-case expected running time of an unsuccessful search for a key k in a hash table storing n keys. Note that this analysis is related to, but distinct from, the analysis we did in the previous chapter. Both are probabilistic, of course, but their probability spaces are different (choosing keys vs. choosing hash functions), and the probability assumptions we are allowed to make are also different, albeit quite similar.

Note that we have made no assumptions about the keys in the hash table, nor about k itself: the only property we used was the universal hash family property, which gave us the upper bound on the probability that the two hash values h ( ki ) and h ( k ) were equal. Because this analysis is true Note that the probability space is now the choice of hash functions, and not choice of keys. This inequality must be true for every pair of keys!

Constructing a universal hash family

Let us round off our two-chapter discussion of hashing by looking at one particular construction of a universal hash family.

We assume that U = { 0, 1, . . . , 2 w -1 } is the set of natural numbers that can be stored in a machine word (so typically w = 32 or w = 64), and that m = 2 M is a power of two. For every odd number a , 0 < a < 2 w , and number (not necessarily odd) b , 0 ≤ b < 2 w -M , we define the following hash function:

Note that these functions are very easy to implement; the first computation ak + b mod 2 w is simply unsigned integer arithmetic, and the second operation is a bit shift, taking the M most significant bits.

Universal Hashing

Now, let us turn to a well-known example of a randomized algorithm: universal hashing. Recall that the simple uniform hashing assumption from the previous chapter says that for any array index 0 ≤ i < m , the probability of choosing a key that hashes to i is 1 m . This assumption made the analysis tractable for us, and in particular ensured a Q ( 1 + a ) average-case running time for the hash table operations. But as we observed, for any hash function we choose, a simple counting argument tells us that at least | U | / m keys must be hashed to the same index. So if any subset of size n of these keys is inserted, any search for a different key that hashes to this same index will take Q ( n ) time.

To cause this worst-case behaviour in practice, a malicious user would study the hash function used and determine such a set of colliding keys. hybrid.question: Compare breadth-first search and depth-first search.
hybrid.ground_truth: BFS explores vertices by increasing distance from the start and is useful for shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS explores deeply before backtracking and is useful for structure discovery such as components or ordering.
hybrid.answer:
Breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS) are both graph traversal algorithms used to explore vertices in a graph, but they differ fundamentally in their traversal strategies:

1. **Traversal Order:**
   - **BFS** explores vertices by visiting all neighbors of the starting vertex first, then the neighbors of those neighbors, and so on. It prioritizes vertices that are closer to the start vertex, moving level by level outward.
   - **DFS** explores as deeply as possible along each branch before backtracking. It visits a vertex, then recursively visits its first unvisited neighbor, continuing down that path until no further unvisited vertices are found along that path.

2. **Data Structure Used:**
   - **BFS** typically uses a queue to manage the vertices to be visited next.
   - **DFS** uses recursion, making use of the function call stack, which naturally follows a last-in-first-out order.

3. **Attributes to Track Status:**
   - In **DFS**, vertices have attributes `started` and `finished` to track whether they have been visited and whether all vertices reachable from them have been fully explored.
   - BFS tracks visited vertices to prevent revisiting but does not use started/finished attributes explicitly.

4. **Running Time:**
   - Both algorithms have similar worst-case running times of Θ(|V| + |E|), where |V| is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges in the graph.

5. **Applications:**
   - **BFS** is used to find the shortest path between two vertices in an unweighted graph by storing parent information to reconstruct the path.
   - **DFS** is useful for detecting cycles in a graph through its started/finished attributes and is often used in tasks like topological sorting and connectivity checks.

6. **Intuitive Understanding:**
   - BFS can be thought of as spreading out from the source vertex in "waves," ensuring the closest vertices are visited first.
   - DFS dives deep into one path, exploring it fully before moving on to alternative paths.

In summary, BFS is typically used when shortest path or level-based exploration is needed, while DFS is favored for tasks requiring full exploration of paths, cycle detection, and connectivity properties [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].

We are now ready to do our first real algorithm on graphs. Consider the central problem of exploring a graph by traversing its edges (rather than relying on direct access of references or array indices). For example, we might want to take a social network, and print out the names of everyone who is connected to a particular person. hybrid.question: Compare adjacency lists and adjacency matrices.
hybrid.ground_truth: Adjacency lists are space-efficient for sparse graphs and efficient for iterating neighbors. Adjacency matrices use more space but allow constant-time edge existence checks.
hybrid.answer:
Adjacency lists and adjacency matrices are two common ways to represent a graph, each with its own advantages and disadvantages:

1. **Representation:**
   - **Adjacency Lists:** Each vertex stores a list of references to its neighboring vertices. The graph stores a collection of these vertices, each with a label and a list of neighbors.
   - **Adjacency Matrices:** The graph is represented as an n-by-n two-dimensional boolean array (where n is the number of vertices). The entry in row i and column j is true if there is an edge between vertex i and vertex j, and false otherwise.

2. **Space Usage:**
   - **Adjacency Lists:** The total space cost is \( \Theta(|V| + |E|) \), where |V| is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges. This is because the graph stores an array of vertices plus the references for edges in adjacency lists. This makes adjacency lists very space efficient for sparse graphs with few edges.
   - **Adjacency Matrices:** The space cost is \( \Theta(|V|^2) \) because it stores the full matrix, including entries for non-edges. This makes adjacency matrices less space efficient when the graph is sparse but potentially more manageable for dense graphs.

3. **Time Complexity for Checking Adjacency:**
   - **Adjacency Lists:** Checking if two vertices i and j are adjacent requires searching through the adjacency list of i to find j, which takes \(O(\min(m, n))\) time, where m is the number of edges and n the number of vertices (worst-case the number of neighbors of i could be up to n-1).
   - **Adjacency Matrices:** Checking adjacency is a constant time operation \(O(1)\) since it's a direct array lookup.

4. **Other Considerations:**
   - Adjacency matrices are symmetric for undirected graphs but not necessarily for directed graphs.
   - Adjacency lists allow easier iteration over neighbors of a vertex without scanning non-neighbors.
   - For graphs where vertices have unique arbitrary identifiers rather than integer indices, adjacency lists can use dictionaries (hash tables) for efficient vertex lookup.

**Summary:**

| Aspect              | Adjacency List                | Adjacency Matrix               |
|---------------------|------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Space usage         | \( \Theta(|V| + |E|) \

hybrid.question: Why is DFS useful for identifying graph structure?
hybrid.ground_truth: DFS records discovery and finish behavior that reveals reachability, connected components, cycles, and ordering relationships in directed or undirected graphs.
hybrid.answer:
Depth-first search (DFS) is useful for identifying graph structure because it systematically explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, which helps reveal connectivity properties and structural features of the graph. Specifically:

1. **Detection of Cycles:** DFS can be modified to detect cycles in a graph efficiently. By keeping track of each vertex's state using two attributes, started and finished, and by recording the parent vertex when visiting a new vertex, DFS can identify when it encounters an already-started vertex that is not its immediate parent. This condition signals a cycle in the graph. Detecting cycles is important because cycles represent redundancy and connectivity characteristics in the graph—the presence or absence of cycles can distinguish between types of graph structures (e.g., trees vs. general graphs) [Source 1, Source 4, Source 7].

2. **Exploring Connected Components:** DFS fully explores the subgraph reachable from a given starting vertex without revisiting vertices, thus revealing connected components. It ensures that all vertices connected to the start vertex are visited and marked, helping understand how the graph is partitioned into components. The recursive nature of DFS and the use of started/finished status attributes allow a formal analysis and proof of its correctness in visiting all connected vertices [Source 2, Source 3].

3. **Runtime Efficiency:** DFS runs in \( \Theta(|V| + |E|) \) time, making it an efficient tool to analyze graph structure even for large graphs [Source 4].

4. **Parent Tracking for Structural Insights:** By storing parent vertices during traversal, DFS helps reconstruct paths and understand ancestor-descendant relationships, which are crucial for understanding hierarchical and cyclical structures within the graph [Source 1, Source 7].

In summary, DFS provides a structured and efficient approach to revealing key structural properties of graphs, including connectedness and cycles, which are fundamental to understanding and analyzing graph topology and behavior.

hybrid.question: What is a minimum spanning tree?
hybrid.ground_truth: A minimum spanning tree is a set of edges connecting all vertices of a connected weighted graph with no cycles and minimum total edge weight.
hybrid.answer:
A minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected weighted graph \( G = (V, E) \) is a subset of edges \( E' \subseteq E \) such that the graph \( (V, E') \) forms a tree (a connected graph with no cycles) and the sum of the weights of the edges in \( E' \) is minimized. In other words, an MST connects all vertices together with the least total edge weight possible, without creating any cycles [Source 1].

This problem arises when you want to keep the graph connected but remove the redundant edges—those whose removal does not disconnect the graph—while minimizing the total edge weight [Source 8].
contexts:
Definition 6 . 8 (tree) . A tree is a connected graph that has no cycles.

So you can view our goal as taking a connected graph, and identifying a subset of the edges to keep, which results in a tree on the vertices of the original graph.

It turns out that the unweighted case is not very interesting, because all trees obey a simple relationship between their number of edges and vertices: every tree with n vertices has exactly n -1 edges. So finding such a tree can be done quite easily by repeatedly finding cycles and choosing to keep all but one of the edges.

However, the weighted case is more challenging, and is the problem of study in this section.

Definition 6 . 9 (minimum spanning tree) . The Minimum Spanning Tree Problem takes as input a connected weighted graph G = ( V , E ) , and outputs a set of edges E ′ such that the graph ( V , E ′ ) is a tree, and which minimizes the sum of the weights e ∈ E ′ we . We call such the resulting tree

a minimum spanning tree (MST) of G .

Prim's algorithm

The first algorithm we will study for solving this problem is known as Prim's algorithm . The basic idea of this algorithm is quite straightforward: pick a starting vertex for the tree, and then repeatedly add new vertices to the tree, each time selecting an edge with minimum weight that connects the current tree to a new vertex.

We won't prove this here, but please take a course on graph theory if you interested in exploring more properties like this in greater detail.

We won't prove this here, but please take a course on graph theory if you interested in exploring more properties like this in greater detail.

Warning: one difference between this definition of tree and the trees you are used to seeing as data structures is that the latter are rooted, meaning we give one vertex special status as the root of the tree. This is not the case for trees in general.

As with shortest paths, there might be more than one minimum spanning tree of G . We just want to find one.

1 def PrimMST(G): 2 v = pick starting vertex from G.vertices 3 TV = {v} # MST vertices 4 TE = {} # MST edges 5 6 while TV != G.vertices: 7 extensions = { (u, v) in G.edges where exactly one of u, v are in TV } 8 e = edge in extensions having minimum weight 9 TV = TV + endpoints of e 10 TE = TE + {e} 11 12 return TE

This algorithm is quite remarkable for two reasons. The first is that it works regardless of which starting vertex is chosen; in other words, there is no such thing as the 'best' starting vertex for this algorithm. The second is that it works without ever backtracking and discarding an already-selected edge to choose a different one. Let us spend some time studying the algorithm to prove that it is indeed correct.

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Kruskal's algorithm

As a bridge between this chapter and our next major topic of discussion, we will look at another algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem. You might wonder why we need another algorithm at all: didn't we just spend a lot of time developing an algorithm that seems to work perfectly well? But of course, there are plenty of reasons to study more than one algorithm for solving a given problem, much as there is for studying more than one implementation of a given ADT: generation of new ideas or insights into problem structure; improving running time efficiency; different possible directions of generalization. In this particular case, we have a pedagogical reason for introducing this algorithm here as well, as motivation for the final abstract data type we will study in this course.

The second algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem is known as Kruskal's algorithm . It is quite similar to Prim's algorithm, in that it incrementally builds up an MST by selecting 'good' edges one Exercise: why is each edge added at most once?

at a time. Rather than build up a single connected component of vertices, however, it simply sorts edges by weight, and always picks the smallestweight edge that doesn't create a cycle with the edges already selected.

1 def KruskalMST(G): 2 TE = {} 3 sort G.edges in non-decreasing order of weights 4 5 for e in G.edges: # starting with the smallest weight edge 6 if TE + {e} does not have a cycle: 7 TE = TE + {e} 8 9 return TE

hybrid.question: Compare Prim's algorithm and Kruskal's algorithm for finding minimum spanning trees.
hybrid.ground_truth: Prim's algorithm grows one tree by repeatedly adding a cheapest edge from the tree to a new vertex. Kruskal's algorithm sorts edges and adds safe edges that connect different components.
hybrid.answer:
Prim's algorithm and Kruskal's algorithm are two well-known methods for finding minimum spanning trees (MSTs) in connected weighted graphs, but they differ in approach and implementation details:

**Prim's Algorithm:**
- Starts with an arbitrary vertex and grows a single tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that extends the tree to a new vertex.
- Maintains a set of vertices TV that are part of the MST and a set of edges TE.
- At each iteration, considers edges connecting TV to vertices not yet in TV and picks the edge with the smallest weight.
- Does not backtrack or discard previously chosen edges, making it efficient.
- Works regardless of the choice of starting vertex.
- Its correctness relies on two loop invariants: (1) the current edge set forms a tree, and (2) this tree can be extended to a MST.
- Initially may be inefficient if implemented naively (O(mn)) when scanning edges, but can be improved using priority queues.
- Runs in O(n) iterations, where n is the number of vertices, adding one vertex each time until all are included [Source 1, 3, 4, 5, 8].

**Kruskal's Algorithm:**
- Sorts all edges by weight and adds edges one by one in order of increasing weight.
- Adds an edge only if it does not create a cycle with the set of already chosen edges.
- Keeps track of connected components of vertices to quickly determine if an edge will create a cycle, often using a union-find (disjoint set) data structure.
- Initially, each vertex is its own component; when an edge is added, the components of its endpoints are merged.
- The challenge is efficiently checking whether two vertices belong to the same component to avoid cycles.
- The sorting step takes O(|E| log |E|) time where |E| is the number of edges.
- Cycle checks are optimized by connected components data structure rather than repeated graph searches.
- The algorithm stops when all vertices belong to one connected component forming the MST [Source 2, 6, 7].

**Summary of Differences:**
- **Approach:** Prim's builds one growing tree by vertex expansions; Kruskal's builds MST edge-by-edge globally via sorted edges.
- **Data structures:** Prim's commonly uses priority queues for edge weight selection; Kruskal's uses union-find for cycle detection.

So finding such a tree can be done quite easily by repeatedly finding cycles and choosing to keep all but one of the edges.

However, the weighted case is more challenging, and is the problem of study in this section.

Definition 6 . 9 (minimum spanning tree) . The Minimum Spanning Tree Problem takes as input a connected weighted graph G = ( V , E ) , and outputs a set of edges E ′ such that the graph ( V , E ′ ) is a tree, and which minimizes the sum of the weights e ∈ E ′ we . We call such the resulting tree

a minimum spanning tree (MST) of G .

Prim's algorithm

The first algorithm we will study for solving this problem is known as Prim's algorithm . The basic idea of this algorithm is quite straightforward: pick a starting vertex for the tree, and then repeatedly add new vertices to the tree, each time selecting an edge with minimum weight that connects the current tree to a new vertex.

We won't prove this here, but please take a course on graph theory if you interested in exploring more properties like this in greater detail.

Kruskal's algorithm

As a bridge between this chapter and our next major topic of discussion, we will look at another algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem. You might wonder why we need another algorithm at all: didn't we just spend a lot of time developing an algorithm that seems to work perfectly well? But of course, there are plenty of reasons to study more than one algorithm for solving a given problem, much as there is for studying more than one implementation of a given ADT: generation of new ideas or insights into problem structure; improving running time efficiency; different possible directions of generalization. In this particular case, we have a pedagogical reason for introducing this algorithm here as well, as motivation for the final abstract data type we will study in this course.

The second algorithm for solving the minimum spanning tree problem is known as Kruskal's algorithm . It is quite similar to Prim's algorithm, in that it incrementally builds up an MST by selecting 'good' edges one Exercise: why is each edge added at most once?

at a time. Rather than build up a single connected component of vertices, however, it simply sorts edges by weight, and always picks the smallestweight edge that doesn't create a cycle with the edges already selected.

1 def KruskalMST(G): 2 TE = {} 3 sort G.edges in non-decreasing order of weights 4 5 for e in G.edges: # starting with the smallest weight edge 6 if TE + {e} does not have a cycle: 7 TE = TE + {e} 8 9 return TE

Warning: one difference between this definition of tree and the trees you are used to seeing as data structures is that the latter are rooted, meaning we give one vertex special status as the root of the tree. This is not the case for trees in general.

As with shortest paths, there might be more than one minimum spanning tree of G . We just want to find one.

1 def PrimMST(G): 2 v = pick starting vertex from G.vertices 3 TV = {v} # MST vertices 4 TE = {} # MST edges 5 6 while TV != G.vertices: 7 extensions = { (u, v) in G.edges where exactly one of u, v are in TV } 8 e = edge in extensions having minimum weight 9 TV = TV + endpoints of e 10 TE = TE + {e} 11 12 return TE

This algorithm is quite remarkable for two reasons. The first is that it works regardless of which starting vertex is chosen; in other words, there is no such thing as the 'best' starting vertex for this algorithm. The second is that it works without ever backtracking and discarding an already-selected edge to choose a different one. Let us spend some time studying the algorithm to prove that it is indeed correct.

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Theorem 6 . 10 (Correctness of Prim's algorithm) . Let G = ( V , E ) be a connected, weighted graph. Then Prim's algorithm returns a set of edges E ′ such that ( V , E ′ ) is a minimum spanning tree for G.

Proof. The proof of correctness of Prim's algorithm is an interesting one, because it relies on two loop invariants, one of which is straightforward, but the other of which is very neat and unexpected if you haven't seen anything like it before. Here are our two invariants (remember that these are true at the beginning and end of every iteration of the loop):

( 1 ) The graph ( TV , TE ) is a tree.

( 2 ) The tree ( TV , TE ) can be extended by only adding some edges and vertices to a minimum spanning tree of G .

Before we prove that these invariants are correct, let's see why they imply the correctness of Prim's algorithm. When the loop terminates, both of these invariants hold, so the graph ( TV , TE ) is a tree and can be extended to an MST for the input graph. However, when the loop terminates, its condition is false, and so TV contains all the vertices in the graph. This means that ( TV , TE ) must be an MST for the input graph, since no more vertices/edges can be added to extend it into one.

We will omit the proof of the first invariant, which is rather straightforward. The second one is significantly more interesting, and harder to This algorithm doesn't 'make mistakes' when choosing edges.

How does this help us check whether adding an edge creates a cycle or not? This is actually where the choice of data structures is important. Note that we have two sets here, a set of vertices and a set of edges. We'll first use an array to represent these sets, so looking up a particular item or adding a new item takes constant time.

How do we compute extensions , the edges that have one endpoint in TV and one endpoint not in TV ? We can loop through all the edges, each time checking its endpoints; this takes Q ( m ) time. hybrid.question: Why does appending to a dynamic array have constant amortized time even though resizing is expensive?
hybrid.ground_truth: Resizing happens only occasionally. The high cost of copying during a resize is spread over many cheap append operations, yielding constant average cost per append over a sequence.
hybrid.answer:
Appending to a dynamic array has constant amortized time because although resizing the array is expensive when it occurs, these costly resize operations happen very infrequently and are preceded by many inexpensive insertions.

More concretely, a resize happens only when the array is full (i.e., when the number of items is a power of two). At this point, an insertion requires copying all existing elements to a new, larger array, which takes linear time in the current number of elements (2n + 1 array accesses). However, before this expensive resizing insertion, there have been many cheap insertions that each take constant time (accessing just one element) without resizing.

For example, inserting into a full array of length 1024 requires about 2049 array accesses, but this insertion is preceded by 511 insertions into the array of length 1024 that each cost only one array access. When viewed over the entire sequence of operations, the total cost spread evenly over all insertions shows that the average cost per insertion is constant.

This reasoning is formalized by amortized analysis, which calculates the average running time per operation over a sequence. The result is that the costly resizes are "paid for" by the many preceding cheap insertions, and the amortized cost of each insertion is O(1). Thus, appending is efficient on average despite occasional expensive resizes [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

Accounting (banker's) method

Nowlet us perform the analysis again through a different technique known as the accounting method , also known as the banker's method . As before, our setup is to consider a sequence of M insertion operations on our dynamic array. In this approach, we do not try to compute the total cost of these insertions directly, but instead associate with each operation a charge , which is simply a positive number, with the property that the total value of the M charges is greater than or equal to the total cost of the M operations .

You may find it strange that the key variable is the number of operations, not the size of the data structure like usual. In amortized analysis, the size of the data structure is usually tied implicitly to the number of operations performed.

Let us summarize TLB activity during our ten accesses to the array: miss , hit, hit, miss , hit, hit, hit, miss , hit, hit. Thus, our TLB hit rate , which is the number of hits divided by the total number of accesses, is 70%. Although this is not too high (indeed, we desire hit rates that approach 100%), it is non-zero, which may be a surprise. Even though this is the first time the program accesses the array, TLB performance gains benefit from spatial locality . The elements of the array are packed tightly into pages (i.e., they are close to one another in space ), and thus only the first access to an element on a page yields a TLB miss.

Also note the role that page size plays in this example. If the page size had simply been twice as big (32 bytes, not 16), the array access would suffer even fewer misses. As typical page sizes are more like 4KB, these types of dense, array-based accesses achieve excellent TLB performance, encountering only a single miss per page of accesses.

This method often proves more flexible, but also more challenging, than the aggregate method. We must not only come up with a charging scheme for the operation, but also then analyse this scheme to ensure that the total charge added is always greater than or equal to the total cost of the operations. As we saw, this is not the same as arguing that the charge is greater than the cost for an individual operation; some operations might have a far higher cost than charge, but have the excess cost be paid for by previous surplus charges. Creative charging schemes take advantage of this by keeping charges high enough to cover the cost of any future operation, while still being low enough to obtain a good bound on the amortized cost of each operation.

In this chapter, we will study another form of algorithm analysis that offers a new type of refinement of worst-case analysis. To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

One can get around this problem by storing the hash table with a data structure that uses dynamically-allocated memory like a linked list or AVL tree, but then we lose the constant-time addressing feature that we get from storing items in a contiguous block of memory. In this chapter, we will study a variant of arrays called dynamic arrays , which we use to implement a resizable collection of items that supports constant-time addressing and 'efficient' insertion of new items. We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

hits.text:
In this chapter, we will study another form of algorithm analysis that offers a new type of refinement of worst-case analysis. To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

One can get around this problem by storing the hash table with a data structure that uses dynamically-allocated memory like a linked list or AVL tree, but then we lose the constant-time addressing feature that we get from storing items in a contiguous block of memory. In this chapter, we will study a variant of arrays called dynamic arrays , which we use to implement a resizable collection of items that supports constant-time addressing and 'efficient' insertion of new items. We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

Dynamic arrays

hybrid.question: Compare aggregate, accounting, and potential methods in amortized analysis.
hybrid.ground_truth: The aggregate method bounds the total cost of a sequence directly. The accounting method assigns artificial charges to operations. The potential method uses a stored potential function to represent prepaid work.
hybrid.answer:
Based on the provided sources, here is a comparison of the aggregate, accounting, and potential methods in amortized analysis:

1. **Aggregate Method**  
- Concept: Compute the total cost of a sequence of operations and then divide by the number of operations to find the average cost per operation.  
- Approach: Analyze the total cost \( T(M) \) of \( M \) operations collectively rather than individually.  
- Example: For dynamic arrays, the total cost of \( M \) insertions involves counting array accesses, especially during expansions when size reaches powers of two. The total cost grows proportionally to \( M \), so the amortized cost per operation is constant \( O(1) \) [Source 1,4].  
- Strength: Simple and intuitive, directly assesses overall average cost.  
- Limitation: May not provide insight into individual operation costs or the distribution of costs within the sequence.

2. **Accounting (Banker's) Method**  
- Concept: Assign each operation a "charge," which may be greater than the actual cost, accumulating "credits" (or surplus) to pay for more expensive future operations.  
- Approach: Instead of summing costs directly, maintain a running "account" where charges always cover actual costs over the whole sequence, ensuring credits never go negative.  
- Example: For dynamic arrays, each insertion is charged 5 credits. Most insertions use just 1 credit, saving the rest to pay for costly array expansions. The total charge over \( M \) operations is always at least the total cost, again leading to amortized \( O(1) \) cost per operation [Source 1,2,3,8].  
- Strength: More flexible than aggregate method; can handle varying costs by balancing cheap and expensive operations.  
- Limitation: Requires a clever charging scheme and proof that total charges cover total costs.

3. **Potential Method** (not explicitly covered in the extracts, but related to accounting)  
- Concept: Assign a "potential" function to the data structure representing stored work or credits, which can increase or decrease with each operation.  
- Approach: Amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost plus the change in potential. This formalizes the intuitive idea of saving or releasing work across operations.  
- Relation: It generalizes the accounting method by mathematically tracking "credits" through a potential function rather than discrete credits per operation.

hybrid.question: Why does union by rank help tree-based disjoint sets?
hybrid.ground_truth: Union by rank attaches the shallower or lower-rank tree under the higher-rank tree, limiting height growth and making future finds faster.
hybrid.answer:
Union-by-rank helps tree-based disjoint sets by reducing the height of the trees in the data structure, which in turn improves the running time of Find and Union operations.

Specifically, union-by-rank maintains a "rank" attribute for each node, which approximates the height of the tree rooted at that node. When performing a Union, the tree with the smaller rank is attached as a subtree to the root of the tree with the larger rank. This prevents the trees from becoming too tall and unbalanced.

As a result, the maximum height \( h \) of any tree in the data structure is bounded by \( O(\log n) \), where \( n \) is the number of elements in the sets. This logarithmic bound on the height leads to improved worst-case running times for Find and Union operations, reducing them from potentially linear time \( O(n) \) to \( O(\log n) \) [Source 1, Source 2, Source 3, Source 4].

In summary, union-by-rank enforces a balanced merging strategy that keeps tree heights low, which improves the efficiency of disjoint set operations.

Union-by-rank

One idea we borrow from AVL trees is the idea of enforcing some local property of nodes to try to make the whole tree roughly balanced. While we do not have to enforce the binary search tree property here, we are limited in two other ways:

We do not want to have to traverse a full tree every time we perform a U nion .

Nodes only have references to their parent, but not their children (child references turn out to be unnecessary).

Rather than have nodes keep track of their height or balance factor, we will store an attribute called rank , which has the following definition:

Definition 8 . 1 (rank (disjoint sets)) . The rank of a node in a disjoint set tree is defined recursively as follows:

The rank of a leaf is 0 .

The rank of an internal node is one plus the maximum rank of its children.

It is no coincidence that this definition is closely related to the recursive definition of tree height you may have seen before. You may wonder, then, why we don't just use height. Indeed, we could for this section; but for the second heuristic we'll study, we want an attribute that never decreases, even when a tree's height decreases. And so for consistency, we use the same attribute for both heuristics.

hybrid.question: What does path compression do during a find operation?
hybrid.ground_truth: Path compression makes nodes on the search path point closer to the root, often directly to the root, reducing the cost of future find operations.
hybrid.answer:
Path compression during a Find operation restructures the tree by making every node on the path from the input node to the root point directly to the root. Specifically, after locating the root (set representative), the algorithm updates the parent attribute of each node along the path to point directly to this root. This effectively "compresses" the path, reducing its length for future Find operations on these nodes.

The purpose is to optimize subsequent Find operations: while the initial Find operation that does the compression may still take time proportional to the length of the path, all later Find operations on nodes along that compressed path will take constant time because those nodes now directly reference the root.

In summary, path compression ensures that once a Find operation is performed on a node, future Find operations on that node or its ancestors are much faster, achieved by flatting the tree structure along that path [Sources 2, 3, 4].

This is true of caching in general: the fi rst time a query is run, there is no speedup due to previous computations, because there are no previous computations!

What path compression does guarantee is that any subsequent F ind operations on any nodes along the compressed path will take constant time. Whenever you hear a phrase like 'operation makes future operations faster,' you should think about amortized analysis: even if the initial operation is slow, perhaps its running time cost can be amortized across multiple (faster) F ind operations. The key insight is that unlike most other tree operations we have looked at in this course, there is no reason to preserve the structure of the tree during a F ind operation . Because each node in a tree only cares about its set representative, there is no reason a node shouldn't just point directly to it, other than the fact that set representatives change during U nion s. So the path compression heuristic is the following: after the set representative is found, all of the nodes traversed have their parent attribute set to this set representative. In purely tree terms, the tree is restructured so that the node and all of its ancestors are made direct children of the root.

For example, when we create a file, we will have to allocate an inode for that file. The file system will thus search through the bitmap for an inode that is free, and allocate it to the file; the file system will have to mark the inode as used (with a 1) and eventually update the on-disk bitmap with the correct information. A similar set of activities take place when a data block is allocated.

Some other considerations might also come into play when allocating data blocks for a new file. For example, some Linux file systems, such as ext2 and ext3, will look for a sequence of blocks (say 8) that are free when a new file is created and needs data blocks; by finding such a sequence of free blocks, and then allocating them to the newly-created file, the file system guarantees that a portion of the file will be on the disk and contiguous, thus improving performance. Such a pre-allocation policy is thus a commonly-used heuristic when allocating space for data blocks.

Running time analysis for path compression

Despite all this fanfare about path compression, it is important to realize that this heuristic does not improve the speed of a F ind operation that has a long path - this operation still takes time proportional to the length of the path, and the worst-case running time is still Q ( n ) , where n is the number of items in the sets. This is true of caching in general: the fi rst time a query is run, there is no speedup due to previous computations, because there are no previous computations!

What path compression does guarantee is that any subsequent F ind operations on any nodes along the compressed path will take constant time. Whenever you hear a phrase like 'operation makes future operations faster,' you should think about amortized analysis: even if the initial operation is slow, perhaps its running time cost can be amortized across multiple (faster) F ind operations. And it turns out that with the path compression heuristic, the amortized running time of F ind operations has a substantial improvement over the worst-case Q ( n ) bound. We will only perform a special case of the full analysis here. You'll find that this is sufficient to get the general idea, while being able to ignore some extra parameters that come with the most generalized version.

One reminder before we go into the proof. This proof uses the notion of node rank from the previous section, with one important clarification: node rank is only updated during a merge operation, and only if the node is the new root of the union tree . This is quite important because path compression can cause tree height to decrease, so keep in mind that rank is not the same as height, and does not change for any node during F ind . We have seen that both union-by-rank and path compression can each be used to improve the efficiency of the F ind operation. We have performed the analysis on them separately, but what happens when we apply both heuristics at once? This is not merely an academic matter: we have seen that it is extremely straightforward to implement each one, and because union-by-rank involves a change to U nion and path compression involves a change to F ind , it is very easy to combine them in a single implementation.

The challenge here is performing the running time analysis on the combined heuristics. We can make some simple observations:

The worst-case bound of Q ( log n ) for F ind from union-by-rank still applies, since it is possible to do a bunch of U nion s, and then a single F ind on a leaf when the tree has height Q ( log n ) .

It is actually quite remarkable that the size of each |M i | doesn't depend on i itself.

For example, when we create a file, we will have to allocate an inode for that file. The file system will thus search through the bitmap for an inode that is free, and allocate it to the file; the file system will have to mark the inode as used (with a 1) and eventually update the on-disk bitmap with the correct information. A similar set of activities take place when a data block is allocated.

Some other considerations might also come into play when allocating data blocks for a new file. For example, some Linux file systems, such as ext2 and ext3, will look for a sequence of blocks (say 8) that are free when a new file is created and needs data blocks; by finding such a sequence of free blocks, and then allocating them to the newly-created file, the file system guarantees that a portion of the file will be on the disk and contiguous, thus improving performance. Such a pre-allocation policy is thus a commonly-used heuristic when allocating space for data blocks.

hybrid.question: Why are union by rank and path compression especially powerful when combined?
hybrid.ground_truth: Union by rank prevents trees from growing tall, while path compression flattens trees during finds. Together they make disjoint-set operations extremely close to constant amortized time.
hybrid.answer:
Union-by-rank and path compression are especially powerful when combined because each heuristic individually improves the efficiency of the Find operation, and when used together, they result in a very efficient disjoint set implementation whose amortized running time is nearly constant.

Here is why their combination is powerful:

1. **Union-by-rank** ensures a balanced tree structure by always attaching the smaller tree to the root of the larger tree, which guarantees that the rank of any node is at most logarithmic in the number of elements (specifically, at most log n). This prevents trees from becoming too tall, improving worst-case running time bounds to O(log n) for Find.

2. **Path compression** optimizes the Find operation by flattening the structure of the tree whenever Find is executed. This means paths from nodes to the root get shortened drastically for subsequent Find operations, leading to improved amortized performance.

3. When combined, the two heuristics complement each other: union-by-rank restricts the rank (height) of the trees to at most log n, and path compression takes advantage of this smaller height to achieve a better amortized cost for Find. The previous upper bound for Find cost, O(log n), improves to O(log log n) with union-by-rank plus path compression, and then further to O(log* n) by Hopcroft and Ullman, and finally to O(α(n)) (where α is the inverse Ackermann function) by Tarjan—the best known asymptotic bound for this problem.

4. Moreover, Tarjan proved a matching lower bound showing that this amortized cost is optimal up to constant factors. He conjectured that no other heuristics or entirely different algorithms could improve the amortized cost beyond what is achieved by this combination.

5. This conclusion was later confirmed by Fredman and Saks in 1989, who proved that any disjoint-set implementation must have an amortized Find cost of at least Ω(α(n)), showing that the union-by-rank and path compression heuristics combined yield an optimal algorithm for the Find and Union operations in the disjoint-set data structure context.

In summary, combining union-by-rank and path compression results in an algorithm with extremely efficient amortized running time for Find operations—specifically, O(α(n)), which is practically constant for all reasonable input sizes—and this is proven to be asymptotically optimal. This powerful synergy is why the combination is widely used and considered the state-of-the

Our previous heuristic involved some optimization on the U nion operation to get a better bound on the height of the trees in the disjoint set collection. Such mutating operations are a natural place for optimization: given that we are modifying the structure of the sets, it is natural to think about how to best do this. In this section, we will investigate a different heuristic, which performs a mutation operation in a previously read-only operation, F ind . This draws inspiration from the common query optimization of caching , in which the result of a query are saved to make future repetitions of the same query faster. When we perform a F ind operation on a node x , we will explicitly store the resulting set representative by restructuring the tree so that performing a F ind on that same node in the future is guaranteed to run in constant time.

hybrid.question: When would a hash table be preferable to an AVL tree, and when would an AVL tree be preferable?
hybrid.ground_truth: A hash table is preferable for expected fast dictionary operations when ordering is unnecessary. An AVL tree is preferable when worst-case logarithmic guarantees or ordered operations are needed.
hybrid.answer:
A hash table is preferable when you want average-case constant-time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion, particularly when keys can be distributed well by a good hash function. Hash tables with closed addressing typically offer average-case running times of \( Q(1 + \alpha) \), where \(\alpha\) is the load factor (ratio of keys to slots). However, the worst-case search and deletion in hash tables can degrade to \( Q(n) \) if many keys hash to the same index, essentially becoming as slow as a linked list [Sources 3,4].

An AVL tree, on the other hand, provides guaranteed worst-case logarithmic running time \( Q(\log n) \) for search, insertion, and deletion because it maintains a balanced binary search tree structure via the AVL invariant. This balanced structure avoids the poor worst-case scenarios that hash tables might encounter [Sources 1,5,6,7].

In summary:
- Use a hash table when you need very fast average-case operations and can tolerate potential worst-case slowdowns, especially if space allows and the distribution of keys is expected to be uniform.
- Use an AVL tree when worst-case time guarantees are important, as it consistently provides logarithmic time in the worst case, making it suitable for scenarios where predictable performance is critical.

This trade-off is emphasized by the fact that hash tables lose their constant-time advantage if the hash function distribution is poor or the load factor becomes high, whereas AVL trees maintain performance by enforcing balance regardless of key distribution [Sources 1,3,4,7].

4 Dictionaries, Round Two: Hash Tables

We now look at a completely different approach for implementing dictionaries. To get warmed up, consider the following scenario: all of the key-value pairs we wish to store have keys that are numbers 0 through K -1. In this case, we can store these pairs inside an array of length K , and achieve constant time search, insertion, and deletion simply by storing each value at the array index corresponding to its key!

This technique is known as direct addressing , and works well when the number of possible keys (and hence total number of pairs) is small. However, array addressing is only constant time if the entire array has been allocated in memory. Thus as K grows larger, even if the running time of the dictionary operations stays constant, the space required grows linearly in K . In this chapter, we will study a generalized version of direct addressing known as hashing , which allows us to store key-value pairs when the keys aren't necessarily numbers, and using much less space than the number of all possible keys.

In this chapter, we will study another form of algorithm analysis that offers a new type of refinement of worst-case analysis. To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

One can get around this problem by storing the hash table with a data structure that uses dynamically-allocated memory like a linked list or AVL tree, but then we lose the constant-time addressing feature that we get from storing items in a contiguous block of memory. In this chapter, we will study a variant of arrays called dynamic arrays , which we use to implement a resizable collection of items that supports constant-time addressing and 'efficient' insertion of new items. We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

hybrid.question: Compare heapsort and randomized quicksort at a high level.
hybrid.ground_truth: Heapsort uses a heap and guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time. Randomized quicksort has expected O(n log n) time and is often fast in practice, but its worst case is still quadratic.
hybrid.answer:
Heapsort and randomized quicksort differ primarily in their approach to sorting and performance characteristics:

1. **Algorithm type and method**:
   - **Heapsort** is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that uses a binary heap data structure to sort items. It works by first building a heap from the input data and then repeatedly extracting the maximum (or minimum) element to build the sorted output.
   - **Randomized quicksort** is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that sorts by recursively partitioning the list using a pivot element chosen randomly (or equivalently, by randomly permuting the input before sorting). The pivot divides the list into smaller sublists, which are then independently sorted.

2. **Randomization and input assumptions**:
   - Heapsort is deterministic and does not rely on any random choices.
   - Randomized quicksort explicitly uses randomness to avoid poor worst-case scenarios by randomly permuting the input to ensure the pivot choice is effectively random, which mitigates issues with already sorted or nearly sorted inputs that cause worst-case behavior in deterministic quicksort [Sources 5, 6, 7].

3. **Worst-case and average-case running times**:
   - Heapsort has a worst-case runtime of \(O(n \log n)\), which is guaranteed regardless of the input ordering.
   - Deterministic quicksort can have a worst case of \(O(n^2)\), but randomized quicksort achieves an expected (average-case) runtime of \(O(n \log n)\) by randomizing pivot choices or input permutations [Sources 2, 3, 6, 7].
   
4. **Space usage**:
   - The versions of quicksort analyzed here sometimes use linear auxiliary storage in their implementation, although in-place versions exist.
   - Heapsort is usually performed in-place, using only \(O(1)\) auxiliary space.

5. **Practical considerations**:
   - Randomized quicksort tends to perform very well in practice due to good average-case behavior and cache friendliness.
   - Heapsort is more predictable in performance but can be slower in practice compared to quicksort due to less favorable memory access patterns.

In summary, heapsort provides a worst-case guarantee of \(O(n \log n)\) without randomness, while randomized quicksort uses random input permutation to achieve expected running time \(O(n \log n)\), balancing simplicity, efficiency, and robustness to input order [Sources 2,

Huh, this is so simple it almost feels like cheating. The only difference is the application of a random permutation to the input. The correctness of this algorithm is clear: because permuting a list doesn't change its contents, the exact same items will be sorted, so the output will be the same. What is more interesting is talking about the running time of this algorithm.

One important point to note is that for randomized algorithms, the behaviour of the algorithm depends not only on its input, but also the random choices it makes . Thus running a randomized algorithm multiple times on the same input can lead to different behaviours on each run. hybrid.question: What is a mathematical statement?
hybrid.ground_truth: A mathematical statement is a sentence with a definite truth value: it is either true or false.
hybrid.answer:
A mathematical statement (or proposition) is a sentence that can be either true or false in a given context. It is a phrase for which it makes sense to ask whether it is true or false, and it may contain words, symbols, or both. Examples of mathematical statements include "The square root of 9 is 3" (true) and "The function \( f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, f(x) = x^2 \) is a bounded function" (false). Phrases that are not statements do not make sense to be evaluated as true or false, such as "5 + 4" (not a statement, but "5 + 4 = 9" is a true statement) [Source 2, Source 3].

Moreover, some phrases with variables (predicates), like \( x > 0 \), are not themselves statements until values are assigned to the variables or quantifiers such as "for any" or "there exists" are introduced to form complete statements [Source 3, Source 4].

The distinction is important because mathematical work largely consists of proving or disproving such statements [Source 1, Source 3].

Naturally, you might ask yourself, why is the notion of a mathematical statement so important? And why would we ever consider false statements? The answer to the first question is simple. Every claim, proposition and theorem is an example of a mathematical statement. Mathematicians spend most of their time trying to prove (or disprove) statements, and therefore it is crucial that we are able to identify what is a statement, and what is not. It would be meaningless to try and prove a phrase which is not a statement (such as ( a + b )( a -b )).

To answer the second question, keep in mind that when mathematicians attempt to prove a new claim or theorem, they do not know (yet) whether that statement is true or false. This is why we must be prepared to work with statements that are (potentially) false. There are many other reasons for considering false statements. False statements are often used in proofs and in negating phrases in mathematics. We will touch on some of these ideas later.

Quantifiers.

As mentioned before, the phrase ' x 2 > 0' is not a mathematical statement (unless we assign a value to x ). However, we can turn it into a statement as follows.

(i) ' For any real number x , we have x 2 > 0.' or (ii) ' x 2 > 0 for some real number x .'

Words such as 'for any', 'every', 'for all', 'there is', 'there exists', 'for some', etc. are called quantifiers , and are used to turn predicates (sentences with variables) into statements. Quantifiers play an essential role in building mathematical statements. As we have just seen, replacing one quantifier by another can change the meaning of the statement.

Connectives.

A connective is a word (or words) that connects two statements to form a new compound statement .

Here is a list of commonly used connectives in mathematics, their 'official' name, and examples. Can you figure out which of the examples are true statements?

3.2 The Logic Symbols

In mathematics, we often use special symbols to denote logical phrases. These symbols allow us to write compound statements, involving connectives and quantifiers, without using the spoken language. Mathematical statements or predicates are often denoted by an uppercase Latin letter (such as P, Q, R or P ( x ) , Q ( x, y ) for phrases that have variables). However, forming a negation by simply adding the word 'not' (or by putting the negation symbol ¬ in front of it) may be insufficient, and mathematicians often try to simplify negations and make them as explicit as possible. For instance, the statement 'not all cats are black' can be restated as 'some cats are not black'. Here is a more mathematical example.

For this reason, proving theorems can be difficult, at times frustrating, and be a long process. But the journey can nevertheless be exciting, enlightening, and transformative. Discovering a proof, especially after working hard and implementing new ideas, can be extremely rewarding. The need to be creative, produce original ideas, and looking at things in a unique way is at the heart of mathematics. For this reason, proving mathematical statements is far from applying a cook-book recipe, and requires effort, persistence, and risk-taking.

However, even without step-by-step instructions, there are some proof strategies that you should be aware of. These strategies are not algorithms, and cannot be applied blindly to create proofs (even after a suitable strategy has been chosen). Instead, they can be seen as commonly-used approaches, or 'modes of thinking'. Choosing an appropriate strategy for proving a given statement can still be challenging, and even after doing so, implementing that strategy can by tricky. With experience and practice, you will become better in deciding how to tackle mathematical statements and proofs.

Direct Proof.

Most statements in mathematics can be regarded as implications; that is, as having the form P ⇒ Q . P

can be seen as the assumptions (or hypotheses), while Q is what needs to be proved. Some mathematical statements are 'if-and-only-if' statements, but these can be naturally regarded as two implications (as P ⇔ Q is logically equivalent to ( P ⇒ Q ) ∧ ( Q ⇒ P ) ).

In other words, you interpreted the phrase as an if-and-only-if statement ('You will have to pay for my bike if and only if you damage it!'), and consequently were very surprised when your friend demanded that you pay.

This kind of confusion can cause serious problems in mathematics. Precision and accuracy are crucial in mathematical arguments and proofs, and so we have to make sure that all interpret statements in the same way. Therefore, we must use 'if-then' when we actually mean if-then, and 'if-and-only-if' when our statement describes an equivalence .

Each of the phrases (i) and (ii) are mathematical statements. Statement (i) is false, as not every real number satisfies x 2 > 0 (if x = 0, then x 2 = 0). On the other hand, statement (ii) is true, as x 2 > 0 does hold for some real numbers.

Words such as 'for any', 'every', 'for all', 'there is', 'there exists', 'for some', etc. are called quantifiers , and are used to turn predicates (sentences with variables) into statements. Quantifiers play an essential role in building mathematical statements. As we have just seen, replacing one quantifier by another can change the meaning of the statement.

For this reason, proving theorems can be difficult, at times frustrating, and be a long process. But the journey can nevertheless be exciting, enlightening, and transformative. Discovering a proof, especially after working hard and implementing new ideas, can be extremely rewarding. The need to be creative, produce original ideas, and looking at things in a unique way is at the heart of mathematics. For this reason, proving mathematical statements is far from applying a cook-book recipe, and requires effort, persistence, and risk-taking.

However, even without step-by-step instructions, there are some proof strategies that you should be aware of. These strategies are not algorithms, and cannot be applied blindly to create proofs (even after a suitable strategy has been chosen). Instead, they can be seen as commonly-used approaches, or 'modes of thinking'. Choosing an appropriate strategy for proving a given statement can still be challenging, and even after doing so, implementing that strategy can by tricky. With experience and practice, you will become better in deciding how to tackle mathematical statements and proofs.

Direct Proof.

Most statements in mathematics can be regarded as implications; that is, as having the form P ⇒ Q . P

can be seen as the assumptions (or hypotheses), while Q is what needs to be proved. Some mathematical statements are 'if-and-only-if' statements, but these can be naturally regarded as two implications (as P ⇔ Q is logically equivalent to ( P ⇒ Q ) ∧ ( Q ⇒ P ) ).

hybrid.question: Compare an implication with its converse.
hybrid.ground_truth: An implication has the form if P then Q. Its converse is if Q then P, which is a different statement and does not automatically have the same truth value.
hybrid.answer:
An implication is a logical statement of the form \( P \Rightarrow Q \) ("if \( P \), then \( Q \)"). Its truth depends on whether whenever \( P \) is true, \( Q \) is also true.

The **converse** of an implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) is the statement \( Q \Rightarrow P \), which switches the hypothesis and conclusion.

From the notes:

- The implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) means that if \( P \) is true, then \( Q \) must be true.
- Its converse \( Q \Rightarrow P \) says if \( Q \) is true, then \( P \) must be true.
- These two statements are generally *not equivalent*; the truth of one does not guarantee the truth of the other.
- For example, the implication "If it is snowing, then the temperature is less than or equal to 0°C" (i.e., \( P \Rightarrow Q \)) may be true, but its converse "If the temperature is less than or equal to 0°C, then it is snowing" (i.e., \( Q \Rightarrow P \)) is not necessarily true.

In contrast, an implication and its **contrapositive** \( (\neg Q) \Rightarrow (\neg P) \) are logically equivalent, meaning they always have the same truth value, but this is different from the converse.

Thus, in summary:

- \( P \Rightarrow Q \) and its converse \( Q \Rightarrow P \) are *not logically equivalent*.
- \( P \Rightarrow Q \) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive \( (\neg Q) \Rightarrow (\neg P) \), but not to its converse.
  
This distinction is important in logic and mathematical proofs, where proving the contrapositive is often easier than proving the implication directly [Source 1, 2, 4, 8].

hybrid.question: How do you negate a universal statement of the form 'for all x, P(x)'?
hybrid.ground_truth: Its negation is 'there exists an x such that not P(x)'.
hybrid.answer:
To negate a universal statement of the form "for all \( x \), \( P(x) \)"—symbolically written as \( \forall x \, P(x) \)—you replace the universal quantifier \( \forall \) with an existential quantifier \( \exists \) and negate the predicate \( P(x) \). Formally, the negation is:

\[
\neg (\forall x \, P(x)) \equiv \exists x \, \neg P(x)
\]

In words, the negation of "for all \( x \), \( P(x) \)" is "there exists an \( x \) such that \( P(x) \) is not true."

This follows the logical rules related to quantifiers and negation: negating a universal quantifier results in an existential quantifier with negated predicate [Source 2], [Source 6].

For example, if the original statement is "all cats are black," its negation is "there exists a cat that is not black" [Source 7].

Thus:

- Original: \( \forall x, P(x) \) → "For all \( x \), \( P(x) \) is true."
- Negation: \( \exists x \) such that \( \neg P(x) \) → "There exists an \( x \) for which \( P(x) \) is false."

This method allows simplification and explicit negation of statements in mathematical logic [Source 5].

hybrid.question: What is the basic structure of a direct proof of an implication?
hybrid.ground_truth: Assume the hypothesis is true, then use definitions, known results, and logical steps to prove the conclusion.
hybrid.answer:
The basic structure of a direct proof of an implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) is as follows:

1. **Assume the hypothesis \(P\)** is true. This means you start with the assumptions or premises given by \(P\).

2. **Use logical reasoning and previously established results** (such as definitions, theorems, or known facts) based on \(P\).

3. **Derive the conclusion \(Q\)** step-by-step from \(P\) until you reach the statement you want to prove.

In other words, you begin with the assumption \(P\) and through a sequence of logical deductions, show that \(Q\) must also be true. This process relies directly on \(P\) without assuming anything about \(Q\).

For example, if you have an implication that says "If the sum of the digits of a number \(n\) is divisible by 3, then \(n\) is divisible by 3," the direct proof would start by assuming the hypothesis (the sum of digits of \(n\) is divisible by 3), and from that, mathematically show that \(n\) itself must be divisible by 3.

This method is straightforward as it moves directly from \(P\) to \(Q\).

This is summarized in the provided materials as:

- Most mathematical statements can be viewed as implications \(P \Rightarrow Q\).
- A direct proof assumes \(P\) and then logically derives \(Q\) using \(P\) and known results.
- Example: if the sum of digits of an integer \(n\) is divisible by 3, then \(n\) is divisible by 3 [Source 1, Source 2].

Thus, the essential components in a direct proof are:

- Starting with the assumed hypothesis \(P\).
- Logical progression toward the conclusion \(Q\).
- Relying on definitions, axioms, and previously proved theorems.

The proof ends with the statement of the conclusion \(Q\) being shown, often marked by a symbol such as a square □ to denote completion [Source 5].

---

**In brief:**  
A direct proof of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) begins by assuming \(P\) is true and uses deductive reasoning to show \(Q\) is true as a consequence of \(P\) [Source 1, 2].

One simple thing an OS might do is disable interrupts during interrupt processing; doing so ensures that when one interrupt is being handled, no other one will be delivered to the CPU. Of course, the OS has to be careful in doing so; disabling interrupts for too long could lead to lost interrupts, which is (in technical terms) bad.

Operating systems also have developed a number of sophisticated locking schemes to protect concurrent access to internal data structures. This enables multiple activities to be on-going within the kernel at the same time, particularly useful on multiprocessors. 6.5 Summary

Wehave described some key low-level mechanisms to implement CPU virtualization, a set of techniques which we collectively refer to as limited direct execution . The basic idea is straightforward: just run the program you want to run on the CPU, but first make sure to set up the hardware so as to limit what the process can do without OS assistance.

This general approach is taken in real life as well. For example, those of you who have children, or, at least, have heard of children, may be familiar with the concept of baby proofing a room: locking cabinets containing dangerous stuff and covering electrical sockets. When the room is thus readied, you can let your baby roam freely, secure in the knowledge that the most dangerous aspects of the room have been restricted.
