4 Dictionaries, Round Two: Hash Tables

We now look at a completely different approach for implementing dictionaries. To get warmed up, consider the following scenario: all of the key-value pairs we wish to store have keys that are numbers 0 through K -1. In this case, we can store these pairs inside an array of length K , and achieve constant time search, insertion, and deletion simply by storing each value at the array index corresponding to its key!

This technique is known as direct addressing , and works well when the number of possible keys (and hence total number of pairs) is small. However, array addressing is only constant time if the entire array has been allocated in memory. Thus as K grows larger, even if the running time of the dictionary operations stays constant, the space required grows linearly in K . In this chapter, we will study a generalized version of direct addressing known as hashing , which allows us to store key-value pairs when the keys aren't necessarily numbers, and using much less space than the number of all possible keys.

Hash functions

In this chapter, we will study another form of algorithm analysis that offers a new type of refinement of worst-case analysis. To set the stage for this technique, let us return to the context of hash tables from Chapter 4 . Recall that in hashing with open addressing, keys are stored directly in the table itself, with collisions being resolved by iterating through a probe sequence of possible indices until an unoccupied spot is found. In our consideration of this technique, we had an underlying assumption that there would be space for every new key-value pair inserted (and that you'd find such a space with a sufficiently long probe sequence). This implied that the array used to store the pairs was bigger than the number of pairs stored. In general, however, we do not know a priori how many pairs are going to be stored in the hash table, and so it is impossible to predict how large an array to use.

One can get around this problem by storing the hash table with a data structure that uses dynamically-allocated memory like a linked list or AVL tree, but then we lose the constant-time addressing feature that we get from storing items in a contiguous block of memory. In this chapter, we will study a variant of arrays called dynamic arrays , which we use to implement a resizable collection of items that supports constant-time addressing and 'efficient' insertion of new items. We put efficient in quotation marks here because our standard measures of efficiency either won't apply or won't be impressive. Instead, we will define and justify a new type of running time analysis known as amortized analysis under which dynamic arrays are excellent .

Dynamic arrays

Or perhaps not. What if all of the keys get mapped to the same index? In this case, the worst case of search and deletion reduces to the worstcase search and deletion from a linked list, which is Q ( n ) , where n is the number of pairs stored in the hash table. Can we simply pick a hash function that guarantees that this extreme case won't happen? Not if we allow the set of keys to be much larger than the size of the array: for any hash function h , there exists an index i such that at least | U | / m keys get mapped to i by h .

So while the worst-case running time for I nsert is Q ( 1 ) ,, the worst case performance for Search and Delete seems very bad: no better than simply using a linked list, and much worse than the AVL trees we saw in the previous section. However, it turns out that if we pick good hash functions, hash tables with closed addressing are much better than both of these data structures on average .

This adds a constant-time overhead per recursive call, and as before, there are O ( h ) recursive calls made. So the total running time is still O ( h ) .

So far, the analysis is exactly the same as for naïve BSTs. Here is where we diverge to success. As we observed at the beginning of this section, BSTs can be extremely imbalanced, and have height equal to the number of nodes in the tree. This is obviously not true for AVL trees, which cannot have all their nodes on (say) the left subtree. But AVL trees are not perfectly balanced, either, since each node's two subtree heights can differ by 1 . Remember that we have not made any assumptions about the relationship between m , the size of the hash table, and | U | , the total possible number of keys; nor have we said anything about what h actually does. Our current implementation makes the assumption that there are no collisions in the hash function; i.e., that each key gets mapped to a unique array slot. Consider what happens when you try to use the above algorithm to insert two key-value pairs whose hashed keys are the same index i : the first value is stored at index i , but then the second value overwrites it.

Now, if m ≥ | U | , i.e, there are at least as many array slots as possible keys, then there always exists a hash function h which has no collisions. Such hash functions are called perfect hash functions , earning the superlative name because they enable the above naive hash table implementation to be correct. However, this assumption is often not realistic, as we typically expect the number of possible keys to be extremely large, and the array to not take up too much space. More concretely, if m < | U | , then at least one collision is guaranteed to occur, causing the above implementation to fail. The remainder of this chapter will be devoted to discussing two strategies for handling collisions.

Closed addressing ('chaining')

The other strategy used to resolve collisions is to require each array element to contain only one key, but to allow keys to be mapped to alternate indices when their original spot is already occupied. This saves the space overhead required for storing extra references in the linked lists of closed addressing, but the cost is that the load factor a must always be less than 1 , i.e., the number of keys stored in the hash table cannot exceed the length of the array.

In this type of hashing, we have a parameterized hash function h that takes two arguments, a key and a positive integer. The 'first' hash value for a key k is h ( k , 0 ) , and if this spot is occupied, the next index chosen is h ( k , 1 ) , and then h ( k , 2 ) , etc.

Remember that we have not made any assumptions about the relationship between m , the size of the hash table, and | U | , the total possible number of keys; nor have we said anything about what h actually does. hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Compare heapsort and randomized quicksort at a high level.
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Heapsort uses a heap and guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time. Randomized quicksort has expected O(n log n) time and is often fast in practice, but its worst case is still quadratic.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
At a high level, heapsort and randomized quicksort differ in their use of randomness, expected running times, and performance guarantees:

1. **Randomness and Pivot Selection**  
- **Randomized quicksort** incorporates randomness inside the algorithm by randomly permuting the input list before applying standard quicksort. This randomization moves the source of randomness inside the algorithm rather than assuming a random input, allowing the algorithm to make random choices internally. The pivot selection is effectively random, which helps avoid worst-case inputs like sorted lists that degrade regular quicksort's performance [Source 1, Source 4].  
- **Heapsort** is a deterministic algorithm that does not rely on random choices. It uses a heap data structure to systematically sort the array.

2. **Running Time and Performance Guarantees**  
- **Randomized quicksort** has an expected running time of \(O(n \log n)\) regardless of the input, meaning that even in the worst-case input, the average running time over the algorithm's internal randomness is asymptotically \(O(n \log n)\). This means an adversary cannot consistently force the algorithm to take more than \(O(n \log n)\) time per run, although individual runs may take longer [Source 2, Source 8].  
- **Heapsort** guarantees a worst-case running time of \(O(n \log n)\). Unlike randomized quicksort, which only guarantees expected \(O(n \log n)\) time, heapsort guarantees that no input will cause the algorithm to exceed this time bound.

3. **Determinism vs. Randomized Behavior**  
- Heapsort is deterministic with consistent performance and predictable running time on all inputs.  
- Randomized quicksort's runtime varies because of its internal random choices but is highly efficient on average, with an expected running time of \(O(n \log n)\).

In summary, randomized quicksort leverages randomness inside the algorithm to avoid worst-case inputs and achieves \(O(n \log n)\) expected time, while heapsort is a deterministic algorithm guaranteeing \(O(n \log n)\) worst-case time without relying on randomization. Both have the same expected asymptotic running time, but their performance guarantees differ due to the reliance on randomness in randomized quicksort [Source 1, Source 2, Source 4, Source 8].

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: What is a mathematical statement?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: A mathematical statement is a sentence with a definite truth value: it is either true or false.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
A mathematical statement (or proposition) is a sentence that can be either true or false in a given context. It is a phrase for which it makes sense to ask whether it is true or false. A mathematical statement may contain words, symbols, or both. For example, "The square root of 9 is 3" is a true mathematical statement, while "The set {ϕ} is empty" is a false statement. On the other hand, phrases like "Z ∪ {1/2, 1/3}" or "5 + 4" are not mathematical statements because it does not make sense to ask if they are true or false. Statements must be clearly understood within their context because the truth or falsity may depend on it (such as the statement "1+1=0" being false in real numbers but true in a field with two elements) [Source 1, Source 5].

Furthermore, statements can be formed from predicates (phrases with variables) by using quantifiers like "for any" or "there exists," which turn a predicate into a statement that can be true or false. For example, "For any real number x, we have x² > 0" is a statement that is false, while "x² > 0 for some real number x" is a true statement [Source 2, Source 5, Source 6].

In essence, mathematical statements are the fundamental building blocks of mathematical logic, claims, propositions, and theorems, and they are what mathematicians attempt to prove or disprove [Source 2, Source 5].

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Compare an implication with its converse.
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: An implication has the form if P then Q. Its converse is if Q then P, which is a different statement and does not automatically have the same truth value.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
An implication is a logical statement of the form \( P \Rightarrow Q \), which means "if \( P \) then \( Q \)." Its converse is the statement \( Q \Rightarrow P \).

The key difference between an implication and its converse is their logical equivalence. The implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) is **not necessarily logically equivalent** to its converse \( Q \Rightarrow P \). In other words, even if the original implication is true, its converse may be false.

For example, consider the implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \):
- \( P \): "It is snowing"
- \( Q \): "The temperature is less than or equal to 0°C."

The statement "If it is snowing, then the temperature is less than or equal to 0°C" might generally be true, but the converse "If the temperature is less than or equal to 0°C, then it is snowing" need not be true because there could be freezing temperatures without snow [Source 3].

In summary:
- The implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) and its converse \( Q \Rightarrow P \) can have different truth values.
- They are not logically equivalent, meaning one can be true without the other being true.

This contrasts with an implication and its contrapositive \( \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P \), which are logically equivalent—both have the same truth value [Source 1].

Therefore, the implication and converse differ in logical equivalence: the implication does not guarantee the truth of its converse.

Example. Let n ∈ Z . If n 3 is odd, then n is odd.

How can we prove this statement? An odd number has the form 2 k +1 (for some integer k ), so we can start by writing n 3 = 2 k + 1. Our task is to show that n is odd, so we might try to solve for n , which gives n = 3 √ 2 k +1. However, it seems like writing n as 3 √ 2 k +1 is not going to be of any help, and we are stuck!

Fortunately, the contrapositive of the implication 'If n 3 is odd, then n is odd.' is 'If n is even, then n 3 is even.' (an integer which is not odd is even), and is much easier to prove.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: How do you negate a universal statement of the form 'for all x, P(x)'?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Its negation is 'there exists an x such that not P(x)'.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
To negate a universal statement of the form "for all x, P(x)" (written symbolically as ∀x P(x)), you replace it with an existential statement stating that there exists some x for which P(x) is not true. In symbols:

\[
\neg (\forall x\, P(x)) \equiv \exists x\, \neg P(x).
\]

This means the negation of "for all x, P(x)" is "there exists an x such that not P(x)."

This is a standard logical equivalence used to simplify negations of statements involving universal quantifiers, as explained in the notes. For example:

- The negation of "All cats are black" is "Some cats are not black."
- More formally, ∀x P(x) negated becomes ∃x ¬P(x).

This equivalence is given in Source 4 and illustrated in examples there. It is also summarized in the logic symbols table in Source 2. 

Hence, the correct way to negate a universal statement is to assert the existence of a counterexample, i.e., some x for which P(x) fails to hold.

The negation of a statement is its opposite, usually obtained by adding the word ' not '.

For instance, the negation of 'all cats are black' is ' not all cats are black', and the negation of 'being tall implies having back problems' is 'being tall does not imply having back problems'. (b) The negation of P = ( ∀ x ∈ R )[( x 2 +1 < 0) ⇒ (15 < 5)] is ¬ P = ( ∃ x ∈ R )[( x 2 +1 < 0) ∧ (15 ≥ 5)] . For any real number x , x 2 +1 > 0, and hence the implication ( x 2 +1 < 0) ⇒ (15 < 5) is true . We conclude that P is true, and ¬ P is false.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: What is the basic structure of a direct proof of an implication?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Assume the hypothesis is true, then use definitions, known results, and logical steps to prove the conclusion.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
The basic structure of a direct proof of an implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) is as follows:

1. Assume the hypothesis \( P \) is true.
2. Use \( P \) together with definitions, previously established theorems, and logical reasoning to show that the conclusion \( Q \) must also be true.

In other words, you start from the assumptions (or hypotheses) \( P \) and logically derive the statement \( Q \), thereby establishing the implication. This approach involves a straightforward chain of reasoning that connects \( P \) to \( Q \) directly.

For example, a direct proof of the implication "If the sum of the digits of a three-digit number \( n \) is divisible by 3, then \( n \) is divisible by 3" begins by assuming the hypothesis (that the sum of digits is divisible by 3), then uses that assumption to conclude that the number \( n \) itself is divisible by 3 [Source 1], [Source 3].

Thus, the key steps are:
- Assume \( P \).
- Use mathematical reasoning based on \( P \) to conclude \( Q \).

This is the essence of a direct proof of an implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \) [Source 4].

For this reason, proving theorems can be difficult, at times frustrating, and be a long process. But the journey can nevertheless be exciting, enlightening, and transformative. Discovering a proof, especially after working hard and implementing new ideas, can be extremely rewarding. The need to be creative, produce original ideas, and looking at things in a unique way is at the heart of mathematics. For this reason, proving mathematical statements is far from applying a cook-book recipe, and requires effort, persistence, and risk-taking.

However, even without step-by-step instructions, there are some proof strategies that you should be aware of. These strategies are not algorithms, and cannot be applied blindly to create proofs (even after a suitable strategy has been chosen). Instead, they can be seen as commonly-used approaches, or 'modes of thinking'. Choosing an appropriate strategy for proving a given statement can still be challenging, and even after doing so, implementing that strategy can by tricky. With experience and practice, you will become better in deciding how to tackle mathematical statements and proofs.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Compare proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction.
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: A contrapositive proof proves if not Q then not P instead of if P then Q. A contradiction proof assumes the statement is false and derives an impossibility.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
Proof by contrapositive and proof by contradiction are both important proof techniques in mathematics, but they differ in approach and structure.

**Proof by Contrapositive:**
- To prove an implication \( P \Rightarrow Q \), one proves its contrapositive \( \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P \).
- Since \( P \Rightarrow Q \) is logically equivalent to \( \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P \), proving the contrapositive confirms the original statement.
- This method often simplifies proofs because it may be easier to show that if the conclusion is false, then the hypothesis is also false.
- Example: To prove "If \( n^3 \) is odd, then \( n \) is odd," one can instead prove the contrapositive "If \( n \) is even, then \( n^3 \) is even," which is easier to demonstrate [Source 2, 4, 5].

**Proof by Contradiction:**
- To prove a statement \( P \Rightarrow Q \), one assumes that \( P \) is true and \( Q \) is false (i.e., assume \( P \) and \( \neg Q \)), and then derives a contradiction.
- The contradiction arises because the assumption that the statement is false conflicts with known truths like definitions, previously established theorems, or the hypothesis.
- Once the contradiction is found, it follows that the original statement must be true.
- Example: To prove that a certain quadratic equation has no rational solutions, assume the contrary (that a rational solution exists) and show this leads to a contradiction with known properties [Source 3].

**Summary of Differences:**
- Contrapositive proofs transform the original statement into an equivalent contrapositive statement and prove that instead.
- Contradiction proofs start by assuming the negation of the statement to be proven and find a logical inconsistency.
- Contrapositive is a direct approach using an equivalent statement, while contradiction emphasizes showing the impossibility of the statement's negation.
- Both methods rely on logical equivalences but differ subtly in execution and style [Source 1, 3, 4, 5].

In practice, deciding which method to use depends on which proof seems more straightforward—often proving the contrapositive is simpler if the direct proof is complicated, while proof by contradiction is used when assuming the negation leads quickly to a contradiction.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: What are the two main parts of a standard induction proof?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: A standard induction proof has a base case and an induction step, where the induction hypothesis is used to prove the next case.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
The two main parts of a standard induction proof are:

1. **The Base Case**: This is the initial step where you prove the statement is true for the first value in the sequence, often \( n = 1 \). It is usually straightforward and must be done to "push the first domino" in the induction analogy.

2. **The Induction Step**: This involves proving that if the statement holds for a particular case \( k \), then it also holds for the next case \( k+1 \). Formally, you assume the statement is true for \( n = k \) (induction hypothesis) and use this assumption to prove it for \( n = k + 1 \).

Together, these show that the statement is true for all natural numbers in the domain by the principle of mathematical induction [Sources 2, 3].

Mathematical induction is a proof technique, used to prove that an infinite sequence of statements is true (or, equivalently, that a statement holds true for all natural numbers). When dealing with infinitely many statements, there is no way we can prove them all by proving each statement individually. Induction is a tool we can often use to bypass this difficulty.

The Principle of Strong Mathematical Induction (PSMI). Assume that P (1) , P (2) , P (3) , . . . is an infinite sequence of mathematical statements. If (1) P (1) is true, and (2) For any k ∈ N : P (1) , P (2) , . . . , P ( k ) imply P ( k +1), then all the statements in the sequence are true.

As we can see, the only difference between the two principles (PMI and PSMI), is in the induction step (i.e., in condition (2)). In PMI, we need to show that for any k ∈ N , P ( k ) ⇒ P ( k +1) (i.e., that the k -th statement implies the ( k +1)-st). With strong induction, we assume, in the induction step, that all the statements P (1) , P (2) , . . . , P ( k ) are true, and prove, from that assumption, the statement P ( k +1). In other words, our induction hypothesis is stronger , and allows us to use any of the statements for n = 1 , . . . , k in our proof.

As an example, we prove the following theorem.

Theorem 4.5.1. Every natural number n ≥ 2 can be written as a product of prime numbers.

(Note: If n is itself a prime number, we can still view it as a product of prime numbers, by allowing our 'products' to have a single factor.)

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Compare ordinary induction and strong induction.
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Ordinary induction assumes the statement for one previous value to prove the next. Strong induction assumes the statement for all previous relevant values to prove the next.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
Ordinary induction (Principle of Mathematical Induction, PMI) and strong induction (Principle of Strong Mathematical Induction, PSMI) are two closely related methods of mathematical proof that differ mainly in the strength of the induction hypothesis used in the induction step.

- **Ordinary induction (PMI)** requires proving two things:
  1. The base case: \(P(1)\) is true.
  2. The induction step: For any \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), assuming \(P(k)\) is true, then prove \(P(k+1)\) is true.  
In other words, the induction hypothesis assumes the statement for exactly one previous value, \(k\), to prove it for the next value \(k+1\).

- **Strong induction (PSMI)** also requires two steps:
  1. The base case: \(P(1)\) is true.
  2. The induction step: For any \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), assuming *all* statements \(P(1), P(2), \ldots, P(k)\) are true, then prove \(P(k+1)\) is true.  
Here the induction hypothesis is stronger because it assumes the truth of the statement for *all* values up to \(k\), not just for a single \(k\).

**Why strong induction is needed sometimes:**  
Strong induction is necessary when the proof for \(P(k+1)\) cannot be accomplished by just assuming \(P(k)\). For example, in the proof that “every natural number \(n \geq 2\) can be written as a product of primes,” the induction step for \(k+1\) uses the fact that if \(k+1\) is composite, then it can be factored as \(m \cdot \ell\), with both \(m\) and \(\ell\) less than or equal to \(k\). To conclude that \(k+1\) can be written as a product of primes, the induction hypothesis must apply to both \(m\) and \(\ell\) simultaneously, not just to \(k\). This requires assuming the statement holds for all values up to \(k\), so strong induction is used.

Thus, some proofs can be done with ordinary induction, but when the proof relies on multiple previous cases or values smaller than \(k+

The base case seems fine. The sets A and B indeed have k elements each, so applying the induction hypothesis on both is legitimate (the hypothesis can be applied as many times as needed). The problem arises when we claim that ' A and B overlap'. It is true that when S has three elements or more, the intersection A ∩ B is nonempty. However, if S = { x 1 , x 2 } , then A = { x 1 } and B = { x 2 } , which implies that A ∩ B = ϕ , and the argument breaks.

The fact that an argument, that is supposed to hold for all k ∈ N , fails for a single value of k , is enough to invalidate the whole proof!

The authors conjectured that because these features give information about the gradient of vertical wind velocity in two different directions, they allow the controller to select between turning by changing the bank angle or continuing along the same course by leaving the bank angle alone. This allows the glider to stay within a rising column of air. Vertical wind velocity is indicative of the strength of the thermal but does not help in staying within the flow. They found that sensitivity to temperature was of little help. They also found that controlling the angle of attack is not helpful in staying within a particular thermal, being useful instead for traveling between thermals when covering large distances, as in cross-country gliding and bird migration.

Due to the fact that soaring in different levels of turbulence requires different policies, training was done in conditions ranging from weak to strong turbulence. In strong turbulence the rapidly changing wind and glider velocities allowed less time for the controller to react. This reduced the amount of control possible compared to what was possible for maneuvering when fluctuations were weak. Reddy et al. examined the policies Sarsa learned under these different conditions. Common to policies learned in all regimes were these features: when sensing negative wind acceleration, bank sharply in the direction of the wing with the higher lift; when sensing large positive wind acceleration and no torque, do nothing. However, different levels of turbulence led to policy differences. Policies learned in strong turbulence were more conservative in that they preferred small bank angles, whereas in weak turbulence, the best action was to turn as much as possible by banking sharply. Systematic study of the bank angles preferred by the policies learned under the different conditions led the authors to suggest that by detecting when vertical wind acceleration crosses a certain threshold the controller can adjust its policy to cope with different turbulence regimes.

The Principle of Strong Mathematical Induction (PSMI). Assume that P (1) , P (2) , P (3) , . . . is an infinite sequence of mathematical statements. If (1) P (1) is true, and (2) For any k ∈ N : P (1) , P (2) , . . . , P ( k ) imply P ( k +1), then all the statements in the sequence are true.

As we can see, the only difference between the two principles (PMI and PSMI), is in the induction step (i.e., in condition (2)). In PMI, we need to show that for any k ∈ N , P ( k ) ⇒ P ( k +1) (i.e., that the k -th statement implies the ( k +1)-st). With strong induction, we assume, in the induction step, that all the statements P (1) , P (2) , . . . , P ( k ) are true, and prove, from that assumption, the statement P ( k +1). In other words, our induction hypothesis is stronger , and allows us to use any of the statements for n = 1 , . . . , k in our proof.

As an example, we prove the following theorem.

Theorem 4.5.1. Every natural number n ≥ 2 can be written as a product of prime numbers.

The authors conjectured that because these features give information about the gradient of vertical wind velocity in two different directions, they allow the controller to select between turning by changing the bank angle or continuing along the same course by leaving the bank angle alone. This allows the glider to stay within a rising column of air. Vertical wind velocity is indicative of the strength of the thermal but does not help in staying within the flow. They found that sensitivity to temperature was of little help. They also found that controlling the angle of attack is not helpful in staying within a particular thermal, being useful instead for traveling between thermals when covering large distances, as in cross-country gliding and bird migration.

Due to the fact that soaring in different levels of turbulence requires different policies, training was done in conditions ranging from weak to strong turbulence. In strong turbulence the rapidly changing wind and glider velocities allowed less time for the controller to react. This reduced the amount of control possible compared to what was possible for maneuvering when fluctuations were weak. Reddy et al. examined the policies Sarsa learned under these different conditions. Common to policies learned in all regimes were these features: when sensing negative wind acceleration, bank sharply in the direction of the wing with the higher lift; when sensing large positive wind acceleration and no torque, do nothing. However, different levels of turbulence led to policy differences. Policies learned in strong turbulence were more conservative in that they preferred small bank angles, whereas in weak turbulence, the best action was to turn as much as possible by banking sharply. Systematic study of the bank angles preferred by the policies learned under the different conditions led the authors to suggest that by detecting when vertical wind acceleration crosses a certain threshold the controller can adjust its policy to cope with different turbulence regimes.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Why is summation notation useful in proofs?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Summation notation compactly represents repeated addition and makes it easier to state, manipulate, and prove formulas involving indexed sums.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer: Summation notation is useful in proofs because it provides a more efficient and compact way to write long sums. This simplification makes it easier to handle and manipulate expressions involving sums, which frequently appear in mathematical identities or inequalities proven by induction or other methods. Using summation notation helps to organize and clarify the structure of these proofs, especially when dealing with many terms or large sequences [Source 4].

As in the first edition, we chose not to produce a rigorous formal treatment of reinforcement learning, or to formulate it in the most general terms. It emphasizes the difference between random variables, denoted with capital letters, and their instantiations, denoted in lower case. Approximate value functions are deterministic functions of random parameters and are thus also in lower case (e.g., ˆ v ( s, w t ) ≈ v π ( s )). Vectors, such as the weight vector w t (formerly θ t ) and the feature vector x t (formerly φ t ), are bold and written in lowercase even if they are random variables. Uppercase bold is reserved for matrices. In the first edition we used special notations, P a ss ′ and R a ss ′ , for the transition probabilities and expected rewards. One weakness of that notation is that it still did not fully characterize the dynamics of the rewards, giving only their expectations, which is sufficient for dynamic programming but not for reinforcement learning. Another weakness is the excess of subscripts and superscripts. In this edition we use the explicit notation of p ( s ′ , r | s, a ) for the joint probability for the next state and reward given the current state and action. We cover both learning and planning methods for the tabular case, as well as their unification in n -step methods and in Dyna. Many algorithms presented in this part are new to the second edition, including UCB, Expected Sarsa, Double learning, tree-backup, Q ( σ ), RTDP, and MCTS. Doing the tabular case first, and thoroughly, enables core ideas to be developed in the simplest possible setting. The second part of the book (Chapters 9-13) is then devoted to extending the ideas to function approximation. It has new sections on artificial neural networks, the fourier basis, LSTD, kernel-based methods, Gradient-TD and Emphatic-TD methods, average-reward methods, true online TD( λ ), and policygradient methods. The second edition significantly expands the treatment of off-policy learning, first for the tabular case in Chapters 5-7, then with function approximation in Chapters 11 and 12. Mathematical induction is a proof technique, used to prove that an infinite sequence of statements is true (or, equivalently, that a statement holds true for all natural numbers). When dealing with infinitely many statements, there is no way we can prove them all by proving each statement individually. Induction is a tool we can often use to bypass this difficulty.

Mathematical induction is an extremely powerful proof technique in mathematics, for several reasons. First, it is not restricted to specific areas of mathematics, and thus can be used to prove statements in algebra, geometry, number theory, analysis, etc. Secondly, induction is useful at all levels of mathematics. It can be used to prove elementary statements about numbers, as well as advanced statements in, say, topology and modern algebra.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: What is a bijection?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: A bijection is a function that is both injective and surjective, so every element of the codomain is matched with exactly one element of the domain.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
A bijection is a function between two sets that is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto). This means that every element in the first set is mapped to a unique element in the second set, and every element in the second set has a pre-image in the first set. In other words, a bijection establishes a perfect "pairing" or "matching" between the two sets with no elements left unmatched in either set.

More formally, if \( f: A \to B \) is a bijection, then each \( b \in B \) corresponds to exactly one \( a \in A \) such that \( f(a) = b \). The function \( f \) can be inverted to form a function \( f^{-1}: B \to A \), which assigns to each element in \( B \) the unique element in \( A \) that maps to it.

This concept is important in comparing the cardinality (or "size") of sets, especially infinite sets: two sets have the same cardinality if and only if there exists a bijection between them [Source 1, 4, 6].

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Why does a bijective function have an inverse function?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Injectivity ensures each output comes from at most one input, and surjectivity ensures each codomain element is hit. Together, each output corresponds to exactly one input, so an inverse is well-defined.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
A bijective function has an inverse function because it is both one-to-one (injective) and onto (surjective). This means for every element in the codomain, there is exactly one element in the domain that maps to it. Therefore, we can "reverse" the function by assigning each element in the codomain back to its unique element in the domain, defining the inverse function.

More formally, if \( f: A \to B \) is a bijection, then its inverse \( f^{-1}: B \to A \) is defined by assigning to any \( y \in B \) the unique \( x \in A \) such that \( f(x) = y \). This inverse function \( f^{-1} \) "undoes" the effect of \( f \), as applying \( f \) and then \( f^{-1} \) returns you to the starting element in the domain, and vice versa [Source 3, Source 7].

The bijectivity (injectivity and surjectivity) is crucial because:

- Injectivity ensures the function never maps two different elements in the domain to the same element in the codomain, so the inverse is well-defined without ambiguity.
- Surjectivity ensures the entire codomain is covered, so every element has a corresponding element in the domain to map back to.

Thus, a bijection guarantees the existence of a unique inverse function.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: How do bijections help compare the sizes of sets?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: If there is a bijection between two sets, their elements can be paired one-to-one with none left over, so the sets have the same cardinality.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
Bijections help compare the sizes of sets by providing a precise and general method to determine if two sets have the same number of elements, even when the sets are infinite. Formally, two sets \( A \) and \( B \) have the same cardinality (or size) if there exists a bijection—a one-to-one and onto function—between them. This means every element in \( A \) can be paired uniquely with exactly one element in \( B \), and vice versa.

For finite sets, this concept aligns with counting: if a bijection exists, the sets have the same number of elements. For infinite sets, counting is impossible, but bijections still offer a way to compare their size rigorously. For instance, there is a bijection between the natural numbers \( \mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, \dots\} \) and the integers \( \mathbb{Z} = \{-1, -2, -3, \dots\} \) (like \( f(n) = -n \)), showing they have the same cardinality despite being infinite.

In more complex cases, bijections show that intervals of different lengths or sets that look very different have the same cardinality. For example, the open interval \( (0,1) \) and the entire real line \( \mathbb{R} \) have the same cardinality, demonstrated via explicit bijections such as \( f(x) = \tan[\pi(x - 0.5)] \).

Thus, bijections serve as the foundational tool for comparing the size of sets by establishing a one-to-one correspondence, providing a clear, mathematical notion of "same size" that extends naturally from finite to infinite sets [Sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

Question: How do we compare the size of two finite sets A and B ?

The quick answer is (of course): By counting . All we have to do is count the number of elements in A and B , and compare the two resulting numbers. If the numbers are equal, the sets have the same size. Otherwise, one set is larger than the other.

There is, however, another method for comparing sets, which is more important and useful in mathematics.

Imagine, for instance, that in a particular university classroom, every student occupies exactly one seat. If some of the seats in the room are unoccupied, we can immediately conclude that the number of seats is larger than the number of students present in class. There is no need to do any counting at all!

Here is another example. In a dance club, a group of teenagers are dancing on the dance floor. If every guy dances with exactly one girl (and no one is left alone), we can conclude right away, that the number of guys on the dance floor equals the number of girls. Again - no counting is needed. The group of dancers form pairs, each of which consists of exactly one guy and one girl. This perfect matching implies that there is an equal number of guys and girls.

Our interest in the matching method is for a different reason though. In mathematics, we often need to deal with infinite sets (such as intervals on the number line, regions in the plane, etc.). However, for infinite sets, the counting method cannot be applied. Which set is larger, the integers ( Z ) or the closed interval [0 , 1]? Both sets are infinite, and counting the number of elements in each is not possible. Fortunately, the pairing (or matching) method can be carried out, and that is how we proceed. 5

In everyday life, we are often required to compare the number of objects of two sets, and decide which one is larger (or whether they are of equal size). Comparing the size (i.e., the number of elements) of two sets, seems to be a straightforward task. Nevertheless, in order to fully understand the notion of cardinality, it is crucial that we take a closer look at the process of comparing the number of objects in two sets.

Question: How do we compare the size of two finite sets A and B ?

hits.text:
Question: How do we compare the size of two finite sets A and B ?

The quick answer is (of course): By counting . All we have to do is count the number of elements in A and B , and compare the two resulting numbers. If the numbers are equal, the sets have the same size. Otherwise, one set is larger than the other.

There is, however, another method for comparing sets, which is more important and useful in mathematics.

Imagine, for instance, that in a particular university classroom, every student occupies exactly one seat. If some of the seats in the room are unoccupied, we can immediately conclude that the number of seats is larger than the number of students present in class. There is no need to do any counting at all!

Here is another example. In a dance club, a group of teenagers are dancing on the dance floor. If every guy dances with exactly one girl (and no one is left alone), we can conclude right away, that the number of guys on the dance floor equals the number of girls. Again - no counting is needed. The group of dancers form pairs, each of which consists of exactly one guy and one girl. This perfect matching implies that there is an equal number of guys and girls.

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Compare finite cardinality with countable infinite cardinality.
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: A finite set has a natural-number size. A countably infinite set can be put in bijection with the natural numbers, so it is infinite but listable in sequence.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
Finite cardinality refers to the number of elements in a finite set, which is a non-negative integer (e.g., a set with 5 elements has cardinality 5). Finite sets can be counted using ordinary counting methods because their number of elements is limited and well-defined.

Countable infinite cardinality, on the other hand, applies to infinite sets that can be put into a one-to-one correspondence (bijection) with the set of natural numbers \( \mathbb{N} \). Such sets are called countable infinite or simply countable. This means their elements can be arranged in an infinite sequence without repetitions, just like \( \mathbb{N} \) itself. Examples of countable sets include \( \mathbb{N} \) (the natural numbers), \( \mathbb{Z} \) (the integers), the set of rational numbers \( \mathbb{Q} \), and even the set \( \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \) (pairs of natural numbers) [Source 3].

Key differences:
- A finite set has a cardinality that is a finite number, while a countable infinite set has a cardinality equal to that of \( \mathbb{N} \), which is an infinite cardinality.
- Finite cardinalities can be compared by ordinary finite numbers; countable infinite cardinality is a concept that captures "the smallest infinity" in terms of set size.
- Intuition from finite sets may fail for infinite sets. For example, a proper subset of a countably infinite set (like the set of even positive integers) can have the same cardinality as the entire set \( \mathbb{N} \) itself, which is counterintuitive for finite cases [Source 2].

In summary, finite cardinality is simply a finite count of elements, whereas countable infinite cardinality refers to infinite sets whose elements can be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers, indicating they have the same kind of "size" or cardinality as \( \mathbb{N} \) [Sources 1, 2, 3].

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: How should the quantifiers in a statement guide the structure of a proof?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Universal statements usually require proving the claim for an arbitrary element. Existential statements require constructing or identifying a witness. Nested quantifiers determine the order in which arbitrary choices and witnesses must be handled.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
Quantifiers in a mathematical statement are crucial as they determine the scope and nature of the proof strategy. Specifically:

- A universal quantifier (e.g., "for any," "for all," denoted as ∀) means that the statement must be proven for every element in the specified set. To prove a statement of the form (∀x) P(x), one must show that P(x) holds true no matter which x is chosen. This often involves reasoning that applies generally without exceptions.

- An existential quantifier (e.g., "there exists," "for some," denoted as ∃) means that it is sufficient to find at least one example or construct one specific element for which the statement holds. To prove a statement of the form (∃x) P(x), it is enough to provide an example or construction to demonstrate P(x) is true for that particular x.

Thus, the presence and type of quantifier guide the proof structure:

- For universal quantifiers, the proof aims at a general argument that applies to all cases.
- For existential quantifiers, the proof typically involves an example or explicit construction.

Changing the quantifier type drastically affects the meaning and proof. As highlighted, "for any real number x, x² > 0" is a universal statement that is false (since x=0 is a counterexample), while "there exists a real number x such that x² > 0" is an existential statement and is true.

In summary, quantifiers determine whether a proof must be a general argument (universal quantifier) or an example-based proof (existential quantifier), and proper understanding of these is essential for constructing accurate mathematical proofs [Sources 3, 6, 8].

hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Why is it useful to express set relationships using element-wise logic?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: Element-wise logic turns set claims into statements about arbitrary elements, making inclusions, equality, unions, intersections, and complements easier to prove rigorously.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer:
Expressing set relationships using element-wise logic is useful because it helps clarify the meaning and validity of statements about sets by focusing on individual elements. For example, to show that one set is a subset of another (A ⊆ B), we consider an arbitrary element x in A and demonstrate why this element must also belong to B. This approach ensures a precise and rigorous understanding of set inclusions. Moreover, it helps in proving equality of sets by verifying the two subset relations (A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A) based on elements.

Additionally, element-wise reasoning is essential when dealing with special cases like the empty set (ϕ). Since the empty set has no elements, statements involving "for every x in ϕ..." are considered true by default because there are no counterexamples. This subtlety is easier to grasp by focusing on elements.

Overall, element-wise logic provides a clear, step-by-step framework for reasoning about sets, which reduces confusion and aids rigorous mathematical proofs [Source 1], [Source 3], [Source 7].

A set will be normally labeled by an upper-case Roman letter (such as A , B , C , S , T , etc.). We use braces to explicitly list the elements of a set. For instance, if A is a set whose elements are the numbers 1, 7, -1 and 5, and B is a set whose elements are the word 'apple', the letter n , and the number 1 2 , we can write

The symbol ∈ is used to indicate that a particular object belongs to a set. The notation y ∈ C reads ' y is an element (or a member) of the set C '. For example, we can write -1 ∈ A and n ∈ B to indicate that the number -1 belongs to the set A , and that n is a member of the set B (defined above). hybrid_plus_rerank.question: Why must a function be well-defined before proving properties like injectivity or surjectivity?
hybrid_plus_rerank.ground_truth: A function must assign each valid input exactly one valid output before other properties can be meaningful. Without well-definedness, claims about one-to-one or onto behavior may not refer to a legitimate function.
hybrid_plus_rerank.answer: A function must be well-defined before proving properties like injectivity or surjectivity because a well-defined function ensures that each element in the domain is assigned exactly one unique image in the codomain. If a function is not well-defined, it may assign multiple images to the same input or fail to assign an image at all, which violates the fundamental definition of a function. Without this certainty, it doesn't make sense to discuss whether the function is injective (one-to-one) or surjective (onto), because the function itself is not properly established. For example, a function that gives different values depending on how an input is represented (like a rational number in different fraction forms) is not well-defined and thus cannot be meaningfully analyzed for injectivity or surjectivity [Source 5].

(a) The composition of two injections is an injection.

(b) The composition of two surjections is a surjection.

(c) The composition of two bijections is a bijection.

hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.question: In the k-armed bandit setting, what does an action-value estimate represent?
hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.ground_truth: An action-value estimate represents the learner's current estimate of the expected reward obtained by selecting a particular action.
hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.answer:
In the k-armed bandit setting, an action-value estimate represents the estimated expected reward of selecting a particular action based on past experience. Formally, the true value of an action \(a\), denoted \(q^*(a)\), is the expected reward given that action \(a\) is selected. Since the true values are unknown, the estimated action value at time step \(t\), denoted \(Q_t(a)\), serves as an approximation to \(q^*(a)\). The goal is for \(Q_t(a)\) to become close to the true value \(q^*(a)\) through learning from received rewards over time [Source 1, Source 2, Source 5].

Thus, the action-value estimate summarizes what is currently known about the average reward expected from taking an action, guiding the decision to exploit the best-known action or explore others to improve these estimates.

If you knew the value of each action, then it would be trivial to solve the k -armed bandit problem: you would always select the action with highest value. We assume that you do not know the action values with certainty, although you may have estimates. We denote the estimated value of action a at time step t as Q t ( a ). If you maintain estimates of the action values, then at any time step there is at least one action whose estimated value is greatest. We call these the greedy actions. When you select one of these actions, we say that you are exploiting your current knowledge of the values of the actions. If instead you select one of the nongreedy actions, then we say you are exploring , because this enables you to improve your estimate of the nongreedy action's value. Exploitation is the right thing to do to maximize the expected reward on the one step, but exploration may produce the greater total reward in the long run. For example, suppose a greedy action's value is known with certainty, while several other actions are estimated to be nearly as good but with substantial uncertainty. The uncertainty is such that at least one of these other actions probably is actually better than the greedy action, but you don't know which one. If you have many time steps ahead on which to make action selections, then it may be better to explore the nongreedy actions and discover which of them are better than the greedy action. Reward is lower in the short run, during exploration, but higher in the long run because after you have discovered the better actions, you can exploit them many times. Because it is not possible both to explore and to exploit with any single action selection, one often refers to the 'conflict' between exploration and exploitation.

2.4 Incremental Implementation

The action-value methods we have discussed so far all estimate action values as sample averages of observed rewards. We now turn to the question of how these averages can be computed in a computationally efficient manner, in particular, with constant memory and constant per-time-step computation.

To simplify notation we concentrate on a single action. Let R i now denote the reward received after the i th selection of this action , and let Q n denote the estimate of its action value after it has been selected n -1 times, which we can now write simply as

One well-studied approach to balancing exploration and exploitation in k -armed bandit problems is to compute a special kind of action value called a Gittins index . In certain important special cases, this computation is tractable and leads directly to optimal solutions, although it does require complete knowledge of the prior distribution of possible problems, which we generally assume is not available. In addition, neither the theory nor the computational tractability of this approach appear to generalize to the full reinforcement learning problem that we consider in the rest of the book.

The Gittins-index approach is an instance of Bayesian methods, which assume a known initial distribution over the action values and then update the distribution exactly after each step (assuming that the true action values are stationary). In general, the update computations can be very complex, but for certain special distributions (called conjugate priors ) they are easy. One possibility is to then select actions at each step according to their posterior probability of being the best action. This method, sometimes called posterior sampling or Thompson sampling , often performs similarly to the best of the distribution-free methods we have presented in this chapter.

In any specific case, whether it is better to explore or exploit depends in a complex way on the precise values of the estimates, uncertainties, and the number of remaining steps. There are many sophisticated methods for balancing exploration and exploitation for particular mathematical formulations of the k -armed bandit and related problems.

However, most of these methods make strong assumptions about stationarity and prior knowledge that are either violated or impossible to verify in most applications and in the full reinforcement learning problem that we consider in subsequent chapters. The guarantees of optimality or bounded loss for these methods are of little comfort when the assumptions of their theory do not apply.

In this book we do not worry about balancing exploration and exploitation in a sophisticated way; we worry only about balancing them at all. In this chapter we present several simple balancing methods for the k -armed bandit problem and show that they work much better than methods that always exploit. The need to balance exploration and exploitation is a distinctive challenge that arises in reinforcement learning; the simplicity of our version of the k -armed bandit problem enables us to show this in a particularly clear form.

2.2 Action-value Methods

We begin by looking more closely at methods for estimating the values of actions and for using the estimates to make action selection decisions, which we collectively call action-value methods . Recall that the true value of an action is the mean reward when that action is selected. One natural way to estimate this is by averaging the rewards actually received:

Consider the following learning problem. You are faced repeatedly with a choice among k different options, or actions. After each choice you receive a numerical reward chosen from a stationary probability distribution that depends on the action you selected. Your objective is to maximize the expected total reward over some time period, for example, over 1000 action selections, or time steps .

This is the original form of the k-armed bandit problem , so named by analogy to a slot machine, or 'one-armed bandit,' except that it has k levers instead of one. Each action selection is like a play of one of the slot machine's levers, and the rewards are the payoffs for hitting the jackpot. Through repeated action selections you are to maximize your winnings by concentrating your actions on the best levers. Another analogy is that of a doctor choosing between experimental treatments for a series of seriously ill patients. Each action is the selection of a treatment, and each reward is the survival or well-being of the patient. Today the term 'bandit problem' is sometimes used for a generalization of the problem described above, but in this book we use it to refer just to this simple case.

In our k -armed bandit problem, each of the k actions has an expected or mean reward given that that action is selected; let us call this the value of that action. We denote the action selected on time step t as A t , and the corresponding reward as R t . The value then of an arbitrary action a , denoted q ∗ ( a ), is the expected reward given that a is selected:

2.3 The 10-armed Testbed

To roughly assess the relative effectiveness of the greedy and ε -greedy action-value methods, we compared them numerically on a suite of test problems. This was a set of 2000 randomly generated k -armed bandit problems with k = 10. For each bandit problem, such as the one shown in Figure 2.1, the action values, q ∗ ( a ), a = 1 , . . . , 10, were selected according to a normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. Then, when a learning method applied to that problem selected action A t at time step t , the actual reward, R t , was selected from a normal distribution with mean q ∗ ( A t ) and variance 1. These distributions are shown in gray in Figure 2.1. We call this suite of test tasks the 10-armed testbed . For any learning method, we can measure its performance and behavior as it improves with experience over 1000 time steps when applied to one of the bandit problems. This makes up one run . Repeating this for 2000 independent runs, each with a different bandit problem, we obtained measures of the learning algorithm's average behavior.

Figure 2.1: An example bandit problem from the 10-armed testbed. The true value q ∗ ( a ) of each of the ten actions was selected according to a normal distribution with mean zero and unit variance, and then the actual rewards were selected according to a mean q ∗ ( a ), unit-variance normal distribution, as suggested by these gray distributions.

The only complication is that many state-action pairs may never be visited. If π is a deterministic policy, then in following π one will observe returns only for one of the actions from each state. With no returns to average, the Monte Carlo estimates of the other actions will not improve with experience. This is a serious problem because the purpose of learning action values is to help in choosing among the actions available in each state. To compare alternatives we need to estimate the value of all the actions from each state, not just the one we currently favor.

This is the general problem of maintaining exploration , as discussed in the context of the k -armed bandit problem in Chapter 2. For policy evaluation to work for action values, we must assure continual exploration. One way to do this is by specifying that the episodes start in a state-action pair , and that every pair has a nonzero probability of being selected as the start. This guarantees that all state-action pairs will be visited an infinite number of times in the limit of an infinite number of episodes. We call this the assumption of exploring starts .

The assumption of exploring starts is sometimes useful, but of course it cannot be relied upon in general, particularly when learning directly from actual interaction with an environment. In that case the starting conditions are unlikely to be so helpful. The most common alternative approach to assuring that all state-action pairs are encountered is to consider only policies that are stochastic with a nonzero probability of selecting all actions in each state. We discuss two important variants of this approach in later sections. For now, we retain the assumption of exploring starts and complete the presentation of a full Monte Carlo control method.

One way to do this is by specifying that the episodes start in a state-action pair , and that every pair has a nonzero probability of being selected as the start. This guarantees that all state-action pairs will be visited an infinite number of times in the limit of an infinite number of episodes. We call this the assumption of exploring starts .

The assumption of exploring starts is sometimes useful, but of course it cannot be relied upon in general, particularly when learning directly from actual interaction with an environment. In that case the starting conditions are unlikely to be so helpful. The most common alternative approach to assuring that all state-action pairs are encountered is to consider only policies that are stochastic with a nonzero probability of selecting all actions in each state. We discuss two important variants of this approach in later sections. For now, we retain the assumption of exploring starts and complete the presentation of a full Monte Carlo control method.

hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.question: Why are constant step-size action-value updates better suited than sample averages for nonstationary bandit problems?
hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.ground_truth: Sample averages weight all past rewards equally, so they adapt slowly when reward distributions change. Constant step-size updates give more weight to recent rewards, allowing estimates to track nonstationary values.
hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.answer:
Constant step-size action-value updates are better suited than sample averages for nonstationary bandit problems because they give more weight to recent rewards, allowing the estimates to adapt more quickly when the reward probabilities change over time. In contrast, sample averages treat all past rewards equally, which is appropriate for stationary problems but not for nonstationary ones.

The key reason is that with constant step-size updates, the estimate \( Q_{n+1} \) becomes an exponential recency-weighted average of past rewards, where older rewards have exponentially decreasing influence. This is achieved by using a constant step-size parameter \( \alpha \in (0,1] \), which causes weights on past rewards to decay exponentially. Therefore, the estimate focuses more on recent data, which is more relevant in a changing environment. On the other hand, sample averages have a step-size \( 1/n \) that diminishes over time, meaning the method becomes less sensitive to recent changes or trends in the rewards.

To quote the source:

- "As noted earlier, we often encounter reinforcement learning problems that are effectively nonstationary. In such cases it makes sense to give more weight to recent rewards than to long-past rewards. One of the most popular ways of doing this is to use a constant step-size parameter."  

- "Accordingly, this is sometimes called an exponential recency-weighted average." [Source 1]

Thus, constant step-size methods allow for faster adaptation in nonstationary environments by weighting recent rewards more heavily, whereas sample averages are inherently slow to react due to equal weighting of all past rewards. This makes constant step-size updates more appropriate for tracking changing action values in nonstationary bandit problems.

We call this technique for encouraging exploration optimistic initial values . We regard it as a simple trick that can be quite effective on stationary problems, but it is far from being a generally useful approach to encouraging exploration. For example, it is not well suited to nonstationary problems because its drive for exploration is inherently temporary. If the task changes, creating a renewed need for exploration, this method cannot help. Indeed, any method that focuses on the initial conditions in any special way is unlikely to help with the general nonstationary case. The beginning of time occurs only once, and thus we should not focus on it too much. This criticism applies as well to the sample-average methods, which also treat the beginning of time as a special event, averaging all subsequent rewards with equal weights. Nevertheless, all of these methods are very simple, and one of them-or some simple combination of them-is often adequate in practice. In the rest of this book we make frequent use of several of these simple exploration techniques.

The advantage of ε -greedy over greedy methods depends on the task. For example, suppose the reward variance had been larger, say 10 instead of 1. With noisier rewards it takes more exploration to find the optimal action, and ε -greedy methods should fare even better relative to the greedy method. On the other hand, if the reward variances were zero, then the greedy method would know the true value of each action after trying it once. In this case the greedy method might actually perform best because it would soon find the optimal action and then never explore. But even in the deterministic case there is a large advantage to exploring if we weaken some of the other assumptions. For example, suppose the bandit task were nonstationary, that is, the true values of the actions changed over time. In this case exploration is needed even in the deterministic case to make sure one of the nongreedy actions has not changed to become better than the greedy one. As we shall see in the next few chapters, nonstationarity is the case most commonly encountered in reinforcement learning. Even if the underlying task is stationary and deterministic, the learner faces a set of banditlike decision tasks each of which changes over time as learning proceeds and the agent's decision-making policy changes. Reinforcement learning requires a balance between exploration and exploitation.

If you knew the value of each action, then it would be trivial to solve the k -armed bandit problem: you would always select the action with highest value. We assume that you do not know the action values with certainty, although you may have estimates. We denote the estimated value of action a at time step t as Q t ( a ). We would like Q t ( a ) to be close to q ∗ ( a ).

If you maintain estimates of the action values, then at any time step there is at least one action whose estimated value is greatest. We call these the greedy actions. When you select one of these actions, we say that you are exploiting your current knowledge of the values of the actions. If instead you select one of the nongreedy actions, then we say you are exploring , because this enables you to improve your estimate of the nongreedy action's value. Exploitation is the right thing to do to maximize the expected reward on the one step, but exploration may produce the greater total reward in the long run. For example, suppose a greedy action's value is known with certainty, while several other actions are estimated to be nearly as good but with substantial uncertainty. The uncertainty is such that at least one of these other actions probably is actually better than the greedy action, but you don't know which one. If you have many time steps ahead on which to make action selections, then it may be better to explore the nongreedy actions and discover which of them are better than the greedy action. Reward is lower in the short run, during exploration, but higher in the long run because after you have discovered the better actions, you can exploit them many times. Because it is not possible both to explore and to exploit with any single action selection, one often refers to the 'conflict' between exploration and exploitation.

The main difference is that now there are multiple states, each acting like a different bandit problem (like an associative-search or contextual bandit) and the different bandit problems are interrelated. That is, the return after taking an action in one state depends on the actions taken in later states in the same episode. Because all the action selections are undergoing learning, the problem becomes nonstationary from the point of view of the earlier state.

To handle the nonstationarity, we adapt the idea of general policy iteration (GPI) developed in Chapter 4 for DP. Whereas there we computed value functions from knowledge of the MDP, here we learn value functions from sample returns with the MDP. The value functions and corresponding policies still interact to attain optimality in essentially the same way (GPI). As in the DP chapter, first we consider the prediction problem (the computation of v π and q π for a fixed arbitrary policy π ) then policy improvement, and, finally, the control problem and its solution by GPI. Each of these ideas taken from DP is extended to the Monte Carlo case in which only sample experience is available.

hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.question: How can optimistic initial values encourage exploration in action-value methods?
hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.ground_truth: Optimistic initial values make unexplored actions appear better than they really are, so greedy selection tries them. As actual rewards are observed, the estimates become more realistic.
hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.answer:
Optimistic initial values encourage exploration in action-value methods by starting the estimated values of all actions at a level higher than what is realistically expected. For example, instead of initializing all action-values to zero, they can be set to a high positive number like +5, which is much larger than the true action values that might be drawn from a distribution with mean 0. This initial overestimation creates "optimism" that any action could yield high rewards.

Because the initial estimates are very optimistic, the agent is "disappointed" when the rewards received from the first selections are lower than these initial values. This disappointment causes the agent to try different actions to find a better one, leading to more thorough exploration. Over time, as rewards are observed and estimates update downward from their optimistic initial values, the agent gains accurate estimates and converges to the best actions. Even if the agent follows a greedy policy (always selecting the best estimated action), this setup encourages exploration early on since all actions start out seeming promising and need to be sampled multiple times before their estimates converge to true values.

However, this approach works well mainly in stationary problems, where the reward distributions do not change. Since the optimism is only in the initial estimates, the drive for exploration is temporary and may not adapt well if the environment is nonstationary.

In summary, optimistic initial values promote exploration by artificially inflating initial action-value estimates to encourage trying all actions multiple times before settling on the best ones, thereby balancing exploration and exploitation effectively in stationary settings [Source 1, Source 2, Source 3, Source 4].

The only complication is that many state-action pairs may never be visited. If π is a deterministic policy, then in following π one will observe returns only for one of the actions from each state. With no returns to average, the Monte Carlo estimates of the other actions will not improve with experience. This is a serious problem because the purpose of learning action values is to help in choosing among the actions available in each state. To compare alternatives we need to estimate the value of all the actions from each state, not just the one we currently favor.

This is the general problem of maintaining exploration , as discussed in the context of the k -armed bandit problem in Chapter 2. For policy evaluation to work for action values, we must assure continual exploration. One way to do this is by specifying that the episodes start in a state-action pair , and that every pair has a nonzero probability of being selected as the start. This guarantees that all state-action pairs will be visited an infinite number of times in the limit of an infinite number of episodes. We call this the assumption of exploring starts .

The assumption of exploring starts is sometimes useful, but of course it cannot be relied upon in general, particularly when learning directly from actual interaction with an environment. In that case the starting conditions are unlikely to be so helpful. The most common alternative approach to assuring that all state-action pairs are encountered is to consider only policies that are stochastic with a nonzero probability of selecting all actions in each state. We discuss two important variants of this approach in later sections. For now, we retain the assumption of exploring starts and complete the presentation of a full Monte Carlo control method.

2.6 Optimistic Initial Values

All the methods we have discussed so far are dependent to some extent on the initial action-value estimates, Q 1 ( a ). In the language of statistics, these methods are biased by their initial estimates. For the sample-average methods, the bias disappears once all actions have been selected at least once, but for methods with constant α , the bias is permanent, though decreasing over time as given by (2.6). In practice, this kind of bias is usually not a problem and can sometimes be very helpful. The downside is that the initial estimates become, in effect, a set of parameters that must be picked by the user, if only to set them all to zero. The upside is that they provide an easy way to supply some prior knowledge about what level of rewards can be expected.

Initial action values can also be used as a simple way to encourage exploration. Suppose that instead of setting the initial action values to zero, as we did in the 10-armed testbed, we set them all to +5. Recall that the q ∗ ( a ) in this problem are selected from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. An initial estimate of +5 is thus wildly optimistic. But this optimism encourages action-value methods to explore. Whichever actions are initially selected, the reward is less than the starting estimates; the learner switches to other actions, being 'disappointed' with the rewards it is receiving. The result is that all actions are tried several times before the value estimates converge. The system does a fair amount of exploration even if greedy actions are selected all the time.

hybrid_plus_rerank_plus_rewrite.answer:
Epsilon-greedy (ε-greedy) and upper-confidence-bound (UCB) action selection are two methods to balance exploration and exploitation in reinforcement learning, but they differ fundamentally in how they select actions under uncertainty.

**Epsilon-greedy action selection:**
- It selects the greedy action (the action with the highest current value estimate) most of the time, specifically with probability \(1 - \epsilon\).
- With a small probability \(\epsilon\), it selects any of the non-greedy actions at random, without preference.
- This approach guarantees that in the limit, every action will be sampled infinitely often, which ensures convergence of value estimates.
- However, exploration is done indiscriminately for non-greedy actions, regardless of how close their estimates are to the greedy action or how uncertain those estimates are.
- ε-greedy is simple to implement and effective in many settings but can be inefficient since it explores all non-greedy actions equally rather than focusing on the most promising or uncertain ones [Source 2][Source 1][Source 5].

**Upper-Confidence-Bound (UCB) action selection:**
- UCB selects actions based on a combination of their estimated value and an uncertainty bonus that encourages trying actions that have either high estimated value or high uncertainty.
- The selection rule maximizes an expression with two terms: the current estimated value of the action plus a confidence bound term proportional to \(\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{N_t(a)}}\), where \(N_t(a)\) is the number of times action \(a\) was chosen up to time \(t\).
- This confidence term represents the uncertainty or variance in the action-value estimate; it decreases as the action is chosen more often (because \(N_t(a)\) grows).
- The natural logarithm in the numerator ensures the exploration term shrinks slowly but never disappears, balancing exploration over time.
- Hence, UCB systematically favors exploring those actions that are under-sampled or have high uncertainty, which can lead to more efficient discovery of optimal actions.
- UCB often performs better than ε-greedy in problems like the k-armed bandit, but it is more complex to extend to nonstationary problems, large state spaces, or with function approximation in reinforcement learning tasks beyond simple bandits [Source 1][Source 3][Source 4].

**Summary of comparison:**
- ε-greedy explores randomly and uniformly

All the methods formed their action-value estimates using the sample-average technique (with an initial estimate of 0). The upper graph shows the increase in expected reward with experience. The greedy method performed significantly worse in the long run because it often got stuck performing suboptimal actions. If you knew the value of each action, then it would be trivial to solve the k -armed bandit problem: you would always select the action with highest value. We assume that you do not know the action values with certainty, although you may have estimates. We denote the estimated value of action a at time step t as Q t ( a ). We would like Q t ( a ) to be close to q ∗ ( a ).

If you maintain estimates of the action values, then at any time step there is at least one action whose estimated value is greatest. We call these the greedy actions. When you select one of these actions, we say that you are exploiting your current knowledge of the values of the actions. If instead you select one of the nongreedy actions, then we say you are exploring , because this enables you to improve your estimate of the nongreedy action's value. Exploitation is the right thing to do to maximize the expected reward on the one step, but exploration may produce the greater total reward in the long run. For example, suppose a greedy action's value is known with certainty, while several other actions are estimated to be nearly as good but with substantial uncertainty. The uncertainty is such that at least one of these other actions probably is actually better than the greedy action, but you don't know which one. If you have many time steps ahead on which to make action selections, then it may be better to explore the nongreedy actions and discover which of them are better than the greedy action. Reward is lower in the short run, during exploration, but higher in the long run because after you have discovered the better actions, you can exploit them many times. Because it is not possible both to explore and to exploit with any single action selection, one often refers to the 'conflict' between exploration and exploitation.

To form control methods, we need to couple such action-value prediction methods with techniques for policy improvement and action selection. Exploration is needed because there is always uncertainty about the accuracy of the action-value estimates. The greedy actions are those that look best at present, but some of the other actions may actually be better. ε -greedy action selection forces the non-greedy actions to be tried, but indiscriminately, with no preference for those that are nearly greedy or particularly uncertain.
